articles.title: After the midterms, is the AI industry in for a rough two years? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: [jwp-video] Democrats’ historic victories in this week’s U.S. midterm elections could also transform the tech industry. The public voted on 41 data center-related ballot measures on Tuesday — in all but one, the majority voted to impose more restrictions on data center development. And even when data centers weren’t on the ballot directly, they were a major talking point, with newly-elected Democratic governors and congressmembers likely to support additional regulation. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and Anthony Ha discuss what the election will mean for the tech industry moving forward — not just when it comes to data centers (which OpenAI is already trying to rebrand), but also increased government scrutiny of Big Tech. articles.title: Larry’s risky business
articles.summary: Larry Ellison and Oracle have staked their future on a data center deal with OpenAI and a big bet that enterprise AI will pay off.
articles.body: If you want to know whether the AI bubble is bursting, there’s only one publicly traded company that will tell you: Oracle. That’s right, the database company. Oracle has burned its boats and pivoted to AI, but not in any kind of usual way. It is not a foundation model builder like OpenAI or Anthropic, obviously. It’s not quite a neocloud, though it has entered the same bare-metal business as CoreWeave. It is a software-as-a-service company that has made an audacious bet on a very specific future version of AI as Oracle’s traditional business has gracefully declined. It is significantly older than any of its AI competitors, save Microsoft, and it has decided its future involves an enormous compute deal with OpenAI, a company that does not make money. Whether OpenAI is good for its commitments to Oracle depends a lot on how much money it can raise and how quickly it can become profitable. The risk for Oracle is that it may be sinking a lot of money into building data centers for OpenAI, only for OpenAI to be unable to pay Oracle the $300 billion it agreed to in their contract. Oracle and OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment. But the OpenAI play — and the pivot to AI generally — suggests a specific vision: The key place to make money isn’t training foundation models. The real money is inference, or using AI models to output results on data that isn’t in the training set. So the company has looked at some startups’ businesses and decided that they are actually just features that can be added to Oracle’s existing capabilities — which is pretty much what Oracle has been up to for the entirety of its existence. Oracle, of course, is already an enterprise business, so it has the existing relationships and large salesforce to go out there and sell its vision, one that suggests there isn’t much room for the AI stack to fragment. Rather, it will consolidate under existing players. Oracle intends to be the dominant player in that game. Wall Street wants to bet on AI, and it can’t bet on OpenAI because it’s not public yet. So the best way to do it now is through Microsoft and Oracle. Microsoft has a more complicated business, so it’s not a pure AI bet. Oracle, on the other hand, is cleaner. That means you can take the temperature of the entire AI boom by checking in on how many people are betting Oracle won’t repay its loans on time — those are the credit default swaps. Oracle’s stock price also reacts to assorted and sundry industry events, providing a bellwether about the AI revolution — or the AI bubble, depending on how you view it. But there’s always a tremendous gap between vision and execution, as Oracle’s history shows. Let’s get it out of the way: Oracle founder Larry “Bad Doggy” Ellison is out of his fucking mind. He has a short attention span, a willingness to promise things his engineers have not yet built, a tremendous ego, and a competitive drive that could power every AI data center on Earth and then some. Ellison is nominally the chief technology officer and executive chairman of Oracle, and Clay Magouyrk and Mike Sicilia are nominally the co-CEOs. But Oracle has always been the Larry show, starring Larry, even when he’s busy cheating at yacht races or whatever. Oracle’s move to focus on AI means leaving behind the high-margin, low-growth, low-capital-expenditure database business that is Oracle’s bread and butter to jump to the low-margin, high-growth, high-capex neocloud business that Oracle has taken out $43 billion in debt to build in just fiscal 2026. Why do that? Well, according to Paul Kedrosky, a longtime VC at SK Ventures, Larry got bored. “This is the story of Larry forever,” says Kedrosky. “Whenever he left to go sailing, he’d say, ‘This company’s not as much fun as it used to be.’ The high-level take is that the orthodox company is low-growth and high-margin and makes him feel old and uncool.” In the 1990s, one of the reasons that Oracle became a hot property was Ellison. He was among the various futurists making predictions about what the internet would do to society. In 1996, Ellison appeared on The Oprah Winfrey Show to hype what he called “the network computer.” (As part of the appearance, Oracle promised to give a network computer to each of almost 300 kids at a primary school in Menlo Park.) This was a lightweight device, even one that could be treated as a throwaway, that would connect to applications stored online. If you are thinking, Boy, that sure sounds like a modern phone, you’re right. If you are also thinking, Boy, that sure sounds like the cloud, you’re also right. The network computer flopped. The iPhone, which kicked off the modern era of lightweight, disposable computing devices, was introduced more than a decade later, in 2007. Oracle veered away from its bold vision of the cloud, while a true believer peeled off to form his own company: Marc Benioff, who founded Salesforce in 1999. Amazon’s AWS venture into cloud computing was in 2006, a decade after Ellison had predicted that people wouldn’t need to keep software on their own computers. So why didn’t Oracle lead both of those revolutions, if Ellison saw them coming a decade out? Well, the iPhone was a consumer product, and Oracle made primarily enterprise databases. Oracle knew how to sell to businesses — it’s why they’d so thoroughly stomped competition such as Relational Technology Inc. and Cullinet in the first place — but Ellison didn’t know how to make consumers choose to buy things rather than get forced to use it by their employer. The failure of the network computer also made Ellison weirdly recalcitrant about the cloud. He refused to take a second crack at the idea until 2011, even mocking it as “complete gibberish.” Oracle never really recovered from its lost lead. Despite its strong enterprise software business, it lags Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Alibaba in market share, and is barely ahead of Salesforce. Given Ellison’s competitive streak — one of his biographies is titled Everyone Else Must Fail — this has to sting. The worst part might have been losing to one of Oracle’s biggest rivals, Microsoft. Still, the majority of Oracle’s business, as of its most recent earnings results, is “cloud and software.” The category represented 88 percent of the company’s revenue in the three months ended February 28th, which is the third quarter in Oracle’s 2026 fiscal year. (There are also hardware and services businesses, but for our purposes, they are negligible.) The majority of that is software support, which “substantially all” customers renew every year “in order to continue to benefit from technical support services and the periodic issuance of unspecified updates and enhancements” to the applications and infrastructure they also use. That brought in a shade under $5 billion in Oracle’s third quarter. The next biggest was “cloud infrastructure,” which had revenue of about $4.9 billion. The customer support business had zero percent growth in the third quarter. Its database and applications businesses, though very profitable, aren’t growing and may even be declining, says analyst Gil Luria of DA Davidson. The cloud business, on the other hand, is growing. It’s an “okay business, very fast-growing with low profitability,” says Luria. “Oracle cloud has single-digit margins, maybe at best teens. But they’ve been growing it very fast.” So when ChatGPT launched the modern era of AI hype in Silicon Valley, it was inevitable that Ellison would take an interest. By February 2025, Ellison was telling former UK Prime Minister Tony Blair that AI was “a much bigger deal than the Industrial Revolution, electricity, and everything that’s come before.” In September, Oracle “shocked the markets” with a $300 billion deal with OpenAI to build data centers, one of the largest cloud deals ever. Oracle’s move into the bare-metal business — renting out servers to AI companies — can be thought of as an extension of the cloud business. Having missed the initial run on the cloud, it seems that Ellison has decided Oracle can’t be left out this time. In some ways, Oracle was an obvious partner for OpenAI. It’s one of the few Big Boys that isn’t trying to compete with Nvidia by building its own chips — though it does have a very close relationship with AMD. But there’s one other benefit that probably tickled Ellison, a longtime Microsoft hater who even resorted to sending private detectives to sort through Microsoft’s trash: OpenAI’s biggest partner for compute used to be Microsoft. The deal was pure, flashy, competitive Ellison — and propelled Oracle’s shares to an all-time high. But with the deal came another big personality: Sam Altman, who has a reputation in Silicon Valley as a sociopathic liar with a people-pleasing streak. OpenAI is the Sam Altman show, as became very clear in 2023 when he was briefly deposed as OpenAI’s philosopher-king. Tying Oracle so closely to OpenAI meant that Oracle was no longer the arbiter of its own fate. And indeed, as OpenAI soon announced a series of other massive deals, Oracle’s shares fell. Now, Oracle serves essentially as a public market proxy for betting on OpenAI’s future — for better and for worse. This time when Ellison predicted the future, he wasn’t the sole true believer, points out Nick Patience, the AI lead at the Futurum group. “It’s a more grounded bet” than the network computer, Patience says. Microsoft’s Satya Nadella and Google’s Sundar Pichai have basically the same vision. On the other hand, Ellison is “piggybacking on Sam Altman, which is probably a dangerous place to be,” Patience notes. Oracle’s OpenAI deal was basically kismet. Oracle had been working on a data center in Texas for Elon Musk, a friend of Ellison’s, who made an abrupt about-face when he decided his company xAI could build his own data center faster. Just as Musk left Oracle in the lurch, a LinkedIn message from OpenAI infrastructure chief Peter Hoeschele arrived in the inbox of a sales leader at Oracle, Bloomberg reported. The resulting deal was significantly larger than the one Oracle had been discussing with Musk, with options to expand it further. To fulfill the deal, Oracle will build five very large data centers. “All told, they’ll require millions of chips and consume 4.5 gigawatts of power — more than all the homes in Chicago,” Bloomberg wrote of the deal. Oracle is planning to build them with an initial completion date in 2027, though according to Bloomberg, that has already slipped to 2028. It’s a more aggressive bet than any other major company has made on AI, and one that the less reckless — or perhaps, less desperate — Microsoft shied away from. Oracle’s previous chief executive officer, Safra Catz, was skeptical of the financial benefits of the cloud. It had lower margins and required costly data centers, Bloomberg reported, citing employees who’d heard Catz’s reservations. She was replaced last year, shortly after the OpenAI deal, by Magouyrk and Sicilia, who previously ran Oracle’s cloud business and applications. In the announcement, Ellison, unsubtly, is quoted saying that “Clay and Mike committed Oracle’s Infrastructure and Applications businesses to AI.” Oracle had burned the boats. OpenAI, for its part, needs Oracle for its investment-grade credit rating, notes Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor at Columbia Business School. OpenAI doesn’t have one, and couldn’t support the necessary compute buildout on its own. Effectively, OpenAI is renting Oracle’s creditworthiness. Of the hyperscalers, however, Oracle has the lowest credit rating. It also has the greatest debt load, even before the infrastructure buildout came into play. What’s more, when I say “Oracle is building data centers,” I am doing a little sleight of hand. Unlike Google and Meta, Oracle doesn’t actually build its own data centers. It’s leasing data centers that other companies are building on its behalf. In Abilene, Texas, that’s Crusoe, with whom Oracle has signed a 15-year lease; Oracle committed to paying more than a billion dollars a year despite Crusoe’s relative lack of experience, according to SemiAnalysis., an industry newsletter. Crusoe’s inexperience is a relatively minor risk compared to the much larger one Oracle is taking on OpenAI, which is by far the biggest customer represented in Oracle’s remaining performance obligations (RPOs), which represent how much money Oracle is slated to earn from its existing contracts. Of the $553 billion in RPOs that Oracle reported in its most recent earnings release, more than $300 billion is OpenAI. So how’s OpenAI doing? [Image: Is OpenAI cooked? In November 2025, Sam Altman sent a memo to OpenAI in which he wrote, “I expect the vibes out there to be rough for a bit.” The vibes had been rough for a bit before the memo, actually. There was the whole thing where Altman got booted and then reinstated. Meta raided OpenAI for talent; several key OpenAI players such as Ilya Sutskever, Bob McGrew, and Mira Murati went on to found their own companies. Anthropic, one of OpenAI’s biggest competitors, is also composed of former OpenAI talent. The executive reshuffling is basically constant. That’s not all on the corporate chaos front. Because OpenAI is trying to go public, it had to repeatedly renegotiate its deal with Microsoft. Not only is Microsoft freed up to partner with other companies, like Anthropic — the revenue-sharing agreement between the two companies ends in 2030 (rather than whenever OpenAI hits a development milestone) and the total payments are capped. “OpenAI products will ship first on Azure, unless Microsoft cannot and chooses not to support the necessary capabilities,” Microsoft announced. But OpenAI can now partner with other cloud providers to try to build its enterprise business. OpenAI’s approach to AI is decidedly unfocused, especially in comparison to Anthropic. There’s something of a profit panic as the company tries to figure out how to make money from its scattershot AI enterprises, while Claude Code and Cowork from Anthropic emerged as the winners for enterprise AI spending. Anthropic doesn’t have image generation or video generation products. It has instead stayed laser-focused on the enterprise market. OpenAI has, by contrast, chased the consumer market, exposing itself to other kinds of risk in the process. The company is facing multiple lawsuits from people who say ChatGPT encouraged loved ones to kill themselves — and, in some cases, others. This has, perhaps predictably, resulted in political pressure. Also there’s a lawsuit from Elon Musk over OpenAI’s for-profit arm that — if Musk wins — may threaten its public offering. This degree of chaos does not inspire confidence in Altman’s management skills. And OpenAI, like all AI labs, is a money furnace. Recently, OpenAI projected that it will spend $665 billion by 2030 — $111 billion more in cash burn than it previously predicted. That’s not all. Its gross profit margins last year were lower than the company predicted, as it had to buy last-minute compute to meet demand. OpenAI projects it will be cash-flow positive in 2030, two years later than its rival Anthropic. Both companies are threatening to go public this year. The thing that’s driving up OpenAI’s costs is inference, the very thing Ellison is betting on. This is probably a positive sign for Ellison’s intuitions about AI use, but it might not be the best thing for his partner. OpenAI has promised $1.4 trillion in its contracts. OpenAI recently raised $122 billion. “That could last them a few years,” Luria says. “I am 100 percent sure they can get to $1.4 trillion? Probably not, but they do have money now, and that makes a difference for Oracle.” Luria’s skepticism is understandable. Take Stargate, the flashy data center project that OpenAI announced, Altman standing shoulder to shoulder with Ellison and Donald Trump. The joint venture hasn’t hired staff and isn’t developing any data centers for OpenAI, The Information reported in February, describing Stargate as a “shelved idea.” Earlier this month, The Information discovered several Stargate leaders, including Hoeschele, ditched OpenAI; they washed ashore at Meta. OpenAI didn’t get its planned 10GW of data center capacity from Oracle and SoftBank last year, either. Part of the problem for OpenAI is that its credit wasn’t as good as Oracle’s — so OpenAI just made its deal with Oracle directly. The two companies also made an unusual arrangement where if there was a delay or the project came in over budget, OpenAI and Oracle would share costs. (They also both benefit if things are under budget.) As for the other member of the project, SoftBank has its own OpenAI agreement, which has led to slapfights over who controls the 1GW facility in Milam County, Texas. OpenAI has signed a long-term lease with subsidiary SoftBank Energy, which would develop and own the data center. Between the complications with Oracle and SoftBank, it seems likely that OpenAI doesn’t have the money or the compute to achieve all of its ambitious goals. Despite all that, Altman is targeting a public offering by the end of 2026, The Wall Street Journal reported in January. That may be in doubt now, after the Journal also reported OpenAI missed revenue and user growth targets. “Chief Financial Officer Sarah Friar has told other company leaders that she is worried the company might not be able to pay for future computing contracts if revenue doesn’t grow fast enough,” the Journal wrote, citing anonymous sources. In response, Dealbook analyst Harrison Rolfes issued a note explaining that OpenAI likely won’t go public this year. OpenAI is racing to beat Anthropic and Musk’s xAI, which has been subsumed by SpaceX and is trying to IPO this summer. SpaceX is seeking a valuation of $1 trillion or more. OpenAI’s most recent funding round gave it a valuation of more than $850 billion. Granted, valuations are more art than science, but it’s also the case that if OpenAI were to IPO with that valuation, it would be valued at 28 times its projected 2026 revenue. By way of comparison, Nvidia — a company that is making an actual profit from the AI boom — is valued at 12 times its projected 2026 revenue. OpenAI’s rich valuation, the company’s long way to profitability, and its aim at consumers rather than enterprises may lead some investors to sit out the IPO, The Information reported. If and when the mandatory paperwork associated with an IPO filing is made public, we’ll get a sense of exactly how challenging the environment is for OpenAI — but it seems that OpenAI doesn’t have an easy road to do everything it’s trying to do and still stay solvent. OpenAI is a flaky partner for Oracle. While that’s the largest challenge for Oracle’s data center buildout, it’s not the only risk. Payments on both Oracle’s bonds and its data center leases will occur on a fixed timeline. Anything that slows the buildout threatens Oracle — money will be flowing out on schedule, but if the build doesn’t happen on time, there may not be enough money flowing in. There are a lot of things that could potentially slow Oracle’s mad dash to build data centers: increasing objections from communities near data centers, supply chain risks from Trump’s war on Iran, and energy risks for the same. What’s more, Oracle has data centers in the now-destabilized Middle East, which could lead to surprise costs that have nothing to do with OpenAI, but nonetheless make it harder for Oracle to pay its bills. Increasingly, communities are objecting to the mad rush to build AI data centers, so much so that 11 states are considering moratoriums. In the case of one of Oracle’s attempted data centers in Doña Ana County, New Mexico, the attempt to quickly build a data center by buttering up local officials — without even really consulting the community the facility would be built in — is now facing several lawsuits from a local environmental group. The data center, dubbed Project Jupiter, would emit more greenhouse gases than the state’s two largest cities, Albuquerque and Las Cruces, combined. The state’s land commissioner has rejected an application for a segment of gas pipeline to power the data center. Though construction has already started, it’s still awaiting two air quality permits — and the decision, with an original deadline of April 22nd, has been delayed several months to allow for a public hearing as opposition to the data center has mounted. Another Oracle-OpenAI data center, in Port Washington, Wisconsin, has similarly drawn pushback from locals. Several protesters were arrested at a city council meeting in December, and one was dragged out for chanting “Recall” at the mayor. Construction on this data center is also underway. Among the people who oppose the data center is the comedian Charlie Berens, who has 3 million subscribers to his YouTube channel of mostly Midwestern humor. This data center project also faces lawsuits from locals, including a challenge to tax incentives for the project worth nearly half a billion dollars. An investigation is now taking place about whether meetings that pushed the data center development forward violated open records laws; Port Washington has also been accused of not turning over public records in response to a request. The construction itself, going around the clock to avoid delays, has also irritated neighbors; new rules limit construction time. There are other signs that the OpenAI alliance may be shaky. OpenAI declined to expand the Abilene, Texas, data center it partners with Oracle on, possibly because it doesn’t have the newest clusters of Nvidia chips. It wasn’t just OpenAI who didn’t want to work with Oracle on this; lenders didn’t want to finance an expansion with Oracle as the tenant, according to The Wall Street Journal. Banks have reportedly grown wary of Oracle debt as private credit investors have gotten anxious about their funds. Should Oracle require more money, it may be harder to find. And now that Ellison’s pal Donald Trump has started a war in Iran with no end in sight, new risks are stacking up for data centers broadly — including Oracle’s. The New York Fed has said that supply chains are facing mounting pressure. In particular, Iran’s blockade on the Strait of Hormuz is a threat to the global helium supply; helium is used in manufacturing semiconductors, and there is nothing that can replace it. There is also an aluminum crisis; the material is used in data center server racks and cooling units. Data centers had already driven up the price of aluminum, while also making it more difficult to manufacture aluminum in the US by increasing energy prices. Speaking of energy prices, there is one more obvious problem that has been created by the Iran war: more expensive energy. Infrastructure damage from the war, along with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has sent prices up without spurring new drilling. That may mean increases in the price of other kinds of energy as people seek out alternatives. Expensive energy could turbocharge objections to data center buildouts, as well as making those builds more pricey. It may also force purveyors of compute to raise their prices, which could make AI even more expensive than it already is. On top of all of that, Oracle’s existing data centers are also in greater jeopardy than before Trump went to war. A Dubai data center has been hit by debris already. Iran claims to be proactively targeting data centers from US companies, including Oracle, and has struck several Amazon facilities. Should Iran take out more Oracle hubs, the company may be forced to rebuild those at the same time as it attempts to build its AI centers — leading to a cash crunch. It may also limit revenue. An increase in the cost of construction and energy, a decrease in revenue, or both could make it much harder for Oracle to meet its lease and debt obligations, which are fixed. Repayment of the $43 billion Oracle raised in fiscal 2026 is split up over a series of years, starting in 2029 and ending in 2066, with a total effective interest rate of 4.9 percent. In the next five years, Oracle will have to repay the $9.5 billion it borrowed in fixed-rate notes, plus another $500 million in floating-rate notes, plus interest. This suggests an aggressive view of what the company can accomplish in five years, since we know Oracle isn’t making enough cash right now to cover its operating expenses and capital expenditures. To turn that around, Oracle has to build data centers, fast, to turn its theoretical future revenue into actual money. The bond market has reflected uncertainty about Oracle’s plans. In December, Oracle’s investment-grade notes were trading like junk bonds, because investors feared data centers would be delayed, according to Bloomberg. Also in December, Oracle’s credit default swaps (CDS) — a kind of insurance in the case of a default — got expensive. But by February, investors were feeling better after newly announced financing plans suggested that Oracle would avoid having its credit downgraded. After Oracle’s strong earnings were announced in March, the five-year CDS got cheaper — then, later that month, hit an all-time high, suggesting investors were nervous again. “Oracle’s CDS has become the credit market’s proxy for AI risk,” John Lloyd, global head of multisector credit and a portfolio manager at Janus Henderson Investors, told Bloomberg. In April, another $14 billion of bonds for an Oracle data center were issued in a special purpose vehicle, keeping the debt off Oracle’s balance sheet. Investors have reason to be nervous. More than half of the data centers scheduled to be built this year may be delayed by equipment shortages — or even canceled. While some builders — like Oracle’s partner Crusoe — are refurbishing old transformers or relying on other strategies, uncertainty around the AI buildout has been rising. It’s not all bad news for Oracle. For instance, ByteDance has been renting chips from Oracle to circumvent export prohibitions of Nvidia’s most advanced chips. According to The Information, ByteDance has become one of Oracle’s largest cloud customers. Oracle also has a $2 billion stake in TikTok’s newly spun-off US operations and hosts all of the company’s user data. What’s more, SemiAnalysis has suggested that in addition to deals in Northern Virginia, ByteDance is a major customer of Oracle’s in Southeast Asia. As ByteDance is planning to grow in Southeast Asia, Europe, and Latin America, Oracle will benefit, according to SemiAnalysis. “The scale of the Oracle and Bytedance partnership remains under the radar,” SemiAnalysis noted, rating Oracle’s GPU service as Gold on its most recent ranking chart. Oracle had strong results in its most recent earnings, too. The company did better than expected at keeping its costs low. It also showed strong growth in its cloud infrastructure business, and 90 percent of its database projects were on or ahead of schedule. “A strong record of on-time delivery is evidence of solid execution,” wrote Luke Yang, an analyst with the financial firm Morningstar. Still, Yang said that there was a lot of uncertainty around Oracle, since the AI landscape changes quickly. But more significant than the bare-metal business may be Ellison’s vision of private AI, deployed within databases Oracle already runs. Sure, Oracle has talked about efficiencies from using AI coding tools. That’s not really the big play, though. Oracle already has sensitive data for a number of businesses, including healthcare records. Having an AI software stack means being able to deploy AI agents into that data to better organize it — with fewer concerns about leakage than there would be with general-purpose third-party LLMs. “Training AI models on public data is the largest, fastest-growing business in history,” Ellison said in December, on an earnings call. “AI models reasoning on private data will be an even larger and more valuable business. Oracle databases contain most of the world’s high-value private data.” There’s reason to believe that training is no longer going to be the same kind of growth industry for AI bare-metal providers; inference will be. After all, one line of thinking goes, the big LLMs have already scraped everything available on the web. But that doesn’t really matter for the application of AI to businesses — inference is what they’d want anyway. Maybe they don’t have everything a business might need yet, says Patience, the analyst with Futurum. But it’s clearly where Ellison is heading. “I don’t think he’s early this time,” Patience said, suggesting this moment was unlike the network phone. “A lot of people would have to be completely wrong, so he’s more protected.” Oracle is also a go-to vendor for the Trump administration, Patience points out. Oracle has, for instance, just won a contract with the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to modernize the agency’s data. It also just won a similar contract with the Air Force. And now US government customers can use a number of Oracle services, including its generative AI. This has, perhaps understandably, freaked people out. Oracle has a history of unauthorized data collection — in 2024, it settled a class-action lawsuit claiming that the company illegally compiled “digital dossiers” including where people browsed online, bought gas, banked, and ate, and sold the information to marketers. The same year, Ellison also suggested, in an analyst meeting, that AI and surveillance will make sure that “citizens will be on their best behavior because we’re constantly recording everything that’s going on.” He described a world in which police officers, wearing Oracle body cams, tell their cameras they need two minutes to go to the bathroom. “We’ll turn it off,” Ellison says. “The truth is, we don’t really turn it off. What we do is, we record it so no one can see it. No one can get into that recording without a court order.” And an AI is always watching, Ellison says. “These are the kind of next-generation systems we can build using AI.” And of course, databases are central to the vision. “We need to unify all the national data, put it into a database where it’s easily consumable by the AI model, and then ask whatever question you like,” Ellison said in another speech at the World Governments Summit. “Right now, countries’ data is fragmented.” Ellison’s prophecy is, effectively, government by database. AI tools and government contracts may make it competitive with Palantir, the current AI standard-bearer in assembling government data so the secret police can stalk their victims. This vision is, obviously, bad news for democracy, but it’s great news for Oracle! I find myself curious about whether the company will simply use its private enterprise data to help add, hmmm, efficiencies to its government efforts, making it easier for surveillance-minded authoritarians to track citizens. Oracle has been wooing authoritarian governments, including China, and has suggested that “pretty much every government is going to want a sovereign cloud and a dedicated region for that government.” And because Oracle is so boring, most people may not even recognize it as a threat. Oh, and there’s one more thing. Besides the risk of Oracle snooping into your business, there’s also the possibility of regulatory capture — that is, because Ellison is so tight with the Trumps, what remains of the government watchdogs won’t stop it. That means there’s no one to prevent Oracle doing assorted dirty deeds — but presumably not dirt cheap. This may create some downside risk if, say, Democrats ever win back power, but perhaps Ellison is betting that if he deploys his technology correctly, that simply won’t happen. Which brings me, finally, to Oracle’s core competency: lock-in. A lot of companies remain on Oracle databases because it is difficult and expensive to relocate. If Oracle’s inference is good enough, the company basically becomes Hotel California for anyone who’s put data there — because to leave is to leave the inference behind. Despite some fairly serious risks to Oracle — largely from its OpenAI deal, and to a lesser extent from the war in Iran — the company may be positioned to succeed. The degree to which you have faith in Ellison’s vision is also the degree to which that vision is disquieting. Oracle’s AI buildout doesn’t necessarily make a lot of financial sense; Ellison may royally piss off his shareholders by the time this is all through. But making financial sense has never been Ellison’s strong point. And besides, what’s he going to do, let Microsoft beat him to the hot new technology? In Oracle’s most recent earnings, the AI buildout shows up on the balance sheet as capital expenditures. Its most recent earnings were for the third quarter of fiscal 2026, which ended in February. Oracle spent $39 billion on capital expenditures, more than three times as much as in the previous fiscal year. As a result, the company now has negative free cash flow. Oracle also told investors that it expected to spend a total of $50 billion in capital expenditures in 2026, and that it was forecasting $67 billion in revenue. In fiscal 2027, Oracle expects $90 billion in revenue. The company did not say how much it forecast in capital expenditures. Morgan Stanley analysts suggest Oracle will need “$100 billion or more for 2027 and the first half of 2028,” according to The Wall Street Journal. “Oracle is about execution right now,” says Luria. “The number one thing is the ability to build data centers and deploy capital to create data centers.” The thing to watch for is whether Oracle can get financing. But even if everything goes smoothly on the building front, Ellison still has to deal with Sam Altman. If OpenAI’s chaos gets too out of hand, it may suck in Oracle, too. What happens to Oracle if OpenAI shits the bed? One possibility is that it sacrifices its software stock premium and gets priced like a utility, which is effectively what the bare-metal business is. Like the telecoms from the ’90s internet boom, it (and its bellwether status) fades in significance as the AI-native companies that survive an AI bubble bursting eventually emerge from the wreckage to reshape our society however that may go. It’s not impossible that the company goes bankrupt, if enough things go wrong at the same time. Because for Oracle to be the dastardly surveillance company of Larry Ellison’s dreams, it has to nail the timing. And that’s never been his strong suit.

articles.title: 'We can't get it back' — even Sam Altman worries about who will control AI's future
articles.summary: OpenAI's Sam Altman sees two ways AI could go terribly wrong, and both are unsettling
articles.body:
When you buy through links on our articles, Future and its syndication partners may earn a commission.

Sam Altman spends much of his time explaining how AI could transform the world for the better and pushing back against doomsayers. Nonetheless, the OpenAI CEO has some fairly unsettling ideas about how AI development could lead to a disaster, or disasters plural. He outlined a couple of these nightmares during an episode of the Figuring Out With Raj Shamani podcast in disturbing detail.

The two dystopias stem from almost opposite problems: either humanity losing control of increasingly powerful machines, or one group seizing control of most of the technology.

"One is that there's a loss of control to AI, and we intentionally or accidentally sort of cede control of the future to systems that are unbelievably more capable than we are, and we can't get it back," Altman said. "And the other is like, one person or company or country gets way too powerful relative to everybody else."

The first scenario is less the tired cliché of a robot uprising and more of a soft surrender of humanity's choices to AI until it's impossible to take back any agency from the AI software. The other is a more modern, if still clichéd, speculative-fiction scenario: an overwhelmingly powerful technology controlled by one person or corporation, leaving everyone else at their mercy. They are both endlessly discussed by people in the industry and policymakers, but having Altman issue the warning is still notable.

Altman, through OpenAI and ChatGPT, is one of, if not the central face of AI to those who have heard the bare minimum about the technology and its flaws. Altman believes those capabilities could bring extraordinary benefits, but his comments suggest he's not sanguine about the looming chaos that AI carries as well.

Advanced AI taking over because people cede control has only become a real-world concern in recent years as the technology moved beyond simply answering questions and into decision-making territory. AI agents can already interact with websites and complete complex assignments, and developers are working toward systems that require less and less human supervision. The more responsibility those systems receive, the greater the consequences if their objectives diverge from what people actually intended.

It's important to remember that what we call AI now relies on probability prediction in different forms. While very powerful and leveraging huge amounts of data, it can't actually make judgments like a human, and doesn't have to be malicious to be harmful. That's why models tend to opt for the disastrous choice of using nuclear weapons as a strategy when simulating how to run a nation.

Humans might not understand or approve of how an AI pursues an objective, even if humans issued the task. And if the AI model has enough power and is embedded in enough critical systems, people might not be able to redirect or stop it. After all, an AI system told to reduce gridlock on the road might logically conclude the solution is to remove the roads, or send an order to any Wi-Fi-enabled car to stop operating. That particular scenario is very unlikely, but the fact that it's not actually impossible is unnerving enough.

We're all familiar with the more human problem of technological and industrial monopolies Altman extended to AI in his other apocalyptic warning. Plenty of people have sounded the alarm about how there is already too much power in too few hands with too little regulation. Altman's hands being among them doesn't mean he won't criticize the fact.

"I think it's actually much better for the world for there to be multiple AI efforts with slightly different approaches that are competing with each other and putting out different ways," Altman said. "I also have this like dislike of too intense power concentration. I think that's not what works, so I'm hopeful we don't do that."

Altman's disdain is in some tension with his company's ambitions and actions. Claiming OpenAI is already dominant in several respects, such as AI infrastructure, is an illustration of the dominance he says he worries about.

"I think we have the most users and the best stack from chips to data centers to models to other things that come around that sort of put abundant intelligence into people's hands. I think we have the best brand and the values that people who are going to use this technology want," Altman said. Nonetheless, he claimed, "we want everybody else to succeed, and I think people can feel that from us."

Despite those warnings, Altman remains fundamentally optimistic about where AI is taking humanity. Asked about his children growing up in a world increasingly shaped by the technology, he expressed confidence that people would find ways to adapt. His outlook suggests that he sees AI's risks as serious challenges to manage rather than reasons to abandon its development.

"I don't know what the future's going to look like, but I am comfortable that I have enormous trust in people to figure out how to adapt and thrive and make society better for all of us," Altman said. "I think the world will most likely keep getting much better."

That optimism extends to OpenAI's future plans to apply AI to scientific exploration. He pointed to recent mathematical achievements as evidence that the technology might be approaching a point where it can contribute meaningfully to fundamental research.

"I am extremely excited to see how far we can push AI to discover new science," Altman said. He envisions "a machine that can help us understand the world better, discover the deepest insights in physics, figure out new medical treatments, a new source of energy, things that I think we can't even imagine but that better scientific understanding will enable. I am extremely excited for us to go build that machine."

articles.title: Meta warns that election backlash against data centers could make AI expansion harder
articles.summary: Meta warns that growing political opposition to data centers could threaten future AI investments, as communities push back against massive infrastructure pr...
articles.body:
Meta president Dina Powell McCormick said that the Democratic wins in the midterm elections are going to make it a lot harder for companies to build data centers, adding that the industry has "not done as good a job as we needed to explain the benefits of these investments."

Speaking at the WSJ Tech conference on Wednesday, the Meta exec pointed out that the backlash against data centers — which was very much on the ballot during this election season — was also tied to people's feelings about AI technology overall.

"The visible sort of manifestation of AI is a data center, and it's something that people can say, 'I don't want this in my community,'" she explained. "I think there's an underlying bigger issue, which is how people feel about AI in general."

Meta believes it could turn around the negative consumer sentiment around AI if it's able to demonstrate the value, not only of the data centers coming to local communities, but also in the technology itself.

"The stakes of who builds the technology that cures cancer, that gives access to education, that is also a very fundamental difference … Mark [Zuckerberg, Meta CEO] is very 'long human,' and he's betting on humans more than machines," Powell McCormick explained. "And that's what we mean when we say the future is for everyone. That people should not be left behind. But the way to ensure that is that this technology is democratized, that people have access to it in a very fair and transparent way," she said.

The exec also touted Meta's experience in building data centers, saying that the company has been doing so for 20 years, as it takes a lot of compute power to offer the products it does in the social networking space. Today, the company has data centers in 23 states, she said, and five of them, including one in Texas, are planned as projects of 1 gigawatt or more.

But Meta is now worried that it could lose some of its investments after politicians ran on anti-data-center platforms during the midterms.

"I think it's going to be harder," Powell McCormick said, describing what the future of building data centers looks like. "It has been hard, I should say, but I also think that it's becoming clear what models work, and the states want those models that work."

Specifically, communities only want data centers when it benefits them in some way, she explained, laying out the approach that Meta today uses to close its data center deals in local communities.

Successful projects see Meta paying for its own electricity, directing any tax surpluses as a result of the data centers toward teachers and first responders, keeping the labor force local, and getting bipartisan support for the project, among other things.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO plans run up against a battered Wall Street
articles.summary: Anthropic's IPO plans are clashing with a market rout.
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) is widely expected to launch its initial public offering sometime between now and the end of the month.

But those chances ran into a massive market buzzsaw on Thursday amid a widespread pullback in tech stocks , with names including AMD ( AMD ), Broadcom ( AVGO ), Micron ( MU ), Nvidia ( NVDA ), and Tesla ( TSLA ) leading the declines.

The sharp drop sent the tech-heavy Nasdaq ( ^IXIC ) tumbling more than 5%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) and Dow ( ^DJI ) dropped nearly 4% and more than 3%, respectively.

The rout sent odds of Anthropic filing its IPO by Nov. 30 on prediction market Kalshi plunging from 84% just yesterday to 60% Thursday afternoon. Odds that the company would file by Dec. 31 also fell from 90% to 74%.

Anthropic is expected to fetch a market valuation of between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion when it goes public.

The steep drop on Wall Street comes after Tuesday's election results swept Democrats into power in the House and Senate.

That has raised questions about the nationwide data center build-out, which became a flash point in the lead-up to the election, with President Trump widely supporting the effort.

Democrats, and some Republicans, however, seized on backlash against data centers and AI more broadly, driving concerns that projects could be canceled or otherwise hindered.

Meta ( META ) president Dina Powell McCormick told an audience at the Wall Street Journal's WSJ Tech event on Wednesday that building data centers will be harder following the election results.

On Thursday, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) outlined its latest policy proposals for data centers it owns and operates, including ending non-disclosure agreements with towns and paying the full cost of the electricity it uses and the infrastructure needed to serve the company's facilities.

Anthropic's IPO will test the market's appetite for AI firms, setting the stage for OpenAI's eventual public offering, which is anticipated early next year.

articles.title: Google plans $17 billion Wyoming data center amid rising threats of curbs

Nov 5 (Reuters) - Alphabet's Google will invest $17 billion to build its first data center in Wyoming, the ‌company said on Thursday, pushing ahead with a major ‌AI infrastructure investment as political resistance to data center expansion grows following ​the US midterm elections.

Of the 41 data center-related ballot measures voted on this week, all but one went against data centers, according to Ballotpedia.

Google's facility will be built in partnership ‌with Tallgrass Energy, Black ⁠Hills Energy, American Electric Power and Related Digital.

The project will be powered in part by a ⁠planned 702-megawatt fuel-cell development equipped with carbon capture and storage technology. The fuel cells will be supplied by Bloom Energy.

Wyoming is ​a ​Republican stronghold, where Donald Trump ​won more than 70% of ‌the presidential vote in 2024.

The announcement comes as investors reassess the pace of the AI infrastructure buildout. Wins by candidates opposed to data-center expansion in key Texas and Georgia races during the midterm elections have added to concerns that ‌political resistance could complicate the industry's ​rapid expansion.

Meanwhile, Microsoft has declined to expand ​a Texas data-center ​agreement with AI cloud provider Nscale, with Bloomberg ‌News reporting earlier in the ​day that the ​company planned to tighten oversight of some data-center projects from neocloud providers Nebius, IREN and Nscale.

Shares of Bloom ​Energy also slumped ‌more than 14% on worries that any potential restrictions ​could hit the industry.

articles.title: Blue Owl Sees Gains as Election Results Limit AI Compute Supply
articles.summary: Blue Owl is telling investors that it expects to earn more on its digital infrastructure deals as capital becomes scarcer while warning that a Democratic swe...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Blue Owl is telling investors that it expects to earn more on its digital infrastructure deals as capital becomes scarcer while warning that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could make it harder to add computing capacity.

"We think those spreads are going to continue to widen out for some period of time," said Erik Bissonnette, president of Blue Owl Technology Finance Corp., on its earnings call. "There is no change in the demand for compute. We think the supply for compute will obviously be a little more challenged given the change of what we're seeing and the fallout potentially here from a change in government."

The fund, also known as OTF, is one of Blue Owl Capital Inc.'s two publicly traded business development companies to report their third-quarter results Thursday. With $330 billion in assets, Blue Owl has been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence trade, ranging from the construction of data centers to the financing of chips that power them.

Traders have grown increasingly fearful around whether the massive spending on building out AI's underlying infrastructure can justify the returns. Those concerns have raised borrowing costs for companies in the space, which could make lending more attractive for those still willing to brave the turbulence.

OTF said its compute deals are focused on very short-duration debt. That includes a recent $2.4 billion financing for AI neocloud Iren Ltd., which was the fund's largest new deal in the third quarter.

It is aiming to increase the allocation for such investments to the "high single digits," up from about 2% of the portfolio at fair value currently. Blue Owl says it is focused on investing based on secure cash flows rather than the value of the chips.

But the firm also looked to calm concerns around private credit, including the level of software exposure and the way the private credit firms value their loans, which do not trade publicly.

During the quarter, it exited $1 billion of investments from another one of its non-traded BDCs, Blue Owl Capital Corp. II, as it continues to wind down the vehicle, telling investors that every loan it sold was purchased at or above their marks.

articles.title: OpenAI is stepping back from NDAs for data center projects
articles.summary: OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including a promise to not use NDAs with public officials.
articles.body: Following this week’s midterms where voters resoundingly voiced their opposition to data center expansion, OpenAI today announced new commitments to communities where it is working on data center projects, including that it won’t use non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) with public officials. Many data center projects have come under scrutiny for relying on NDAs to hide discussions between developers and local officials. However, OpenAI says it is now allowing “only narrow protections covering legitimate security information, trade secrets, or proprietary or competitively sensitive information.” In October, Amazon announced it would no longer use NDAs with government agencies it works with on data center projects. OpenAI’s additional commitments include paying “the full cost” of electricity it uses and the “infrastructure needed to serve us.” It will make opportunities for local communities by publishing the jobs it expects to create and by reporting on hiring. And every future “compute campus” (its rebranding phrase for data centers) the company owns and operates will have a “local compact” that includes the commitments and will reflect “local priorities,” OpenAI says.

articles.title: Anthropic launches personal finance feature in Claude, lets users connect bank accounts for money insights
articles.summary: After ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, now AI giant Anthropic has introduced personal finance feature to its chatbot Claude.
articles.body: After ChatGPT-maker OpenAI, now AI giant Anthropic has introduced personal finance feature to its chatbot Claude. Anthropic has announced the roll out of Personal Finance feature for its AI assistant Claude, enabling users to connect bank and card accounts and also ask questions about their finances in natural language. The company also said that the feature is created to help users get to better understand their spending, balances and transactions without switching between multiple banking apps. Presently, the company is rolling out the feature only for beta subscribers on Claude's Pro, Max and Ultra plans in the United States. As per Anthropic, users can now securely connect their financial accounts and also receive answers about their money, with Claude offering explanations in everyday language.Claude Personal Finance feature: What it doesUsers can ask questions such as where their money went this month, whether they are spending more than they earn, or what an APR is and how much interest they have been charged this year. Claude answers from the connected accounts’ balances and transactions, in everyday language, and explains unfamiliar terms. In an example from Anthropic, a user ten days from payday asks where their money went. Claude totals spending across linked accounts and sorts it by category. It then checks previous months, flags a membership renewal, and lists four payments due from checking before payday along with the amount that will be left.Claude can also look across all linked accounts for things that are easy to miss, such as duplicate charges, unexpected fees or a bill that has crept up over the year. Users can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due or a dashboard of chosen numbers, and keep adjusting it.Focus on privacy and securityAnthropic emphasised that the new feature provides read-only access to financial data and cannot move, manage or invest a user's money. The company also noted that Personal Finance is not designed to provide investment advice and that users should verify important figures directly with their banks. Account connectivity is powered by financial data network Plaid, which allows users to authenticate directly with their banks. Anthropic said Claude does not see or request users' banking passwords. For connected accounts, Claude can access information such as account names, balances, credit limits and up to two years of transaction history.The company added that conversations conducted within the Personal Finance hub are not used to train its AI models. Users can also disconnect their accounts at any time, after which Claude can no longer access the associated dataNo ads or product salesAnthropic said Personal Finance carries no ads or sponsored recommendations. It also does not offer credit cards, loans or savings accounts of its own, so users get a straight answer.Getting started and what’s nextUsers who see Personal Finance in Claude’s sidebar can connect one account and ask a question, such as whether they can afford a trip this spring. Setup steps are in the Help Center.Anthropic called the launch a first step. For bigger financial decisions, it said, people are best served by Claude working alongside licensed professionals and regulated firms. The company said it is exploring how to enable that and wants to hear from banks, wealth managers and financial services firms that want to help shape it.You use AI every day. articles.title: OpenAI launches GPT-6 Cyber, finds 81 high-severity Firefox flaws and 948 Linux exploits
articles.summary: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a new artificial intelligence (AI) model designed to help cybersecurity researchers find, validate and fix software
articles.body: OpenAI has launched GPT-6 Cyber, a new artificial intelligence (AI) model designed to help cybersecurity researchers find, validate and fix software vulnerabilities. In its official announcement, the company said the model has already helped uncover 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox and develop working exploits for 948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities. GPT-6 Cyber is claimed to be a major upgrade over GPT-5.6 Cyber, with improved vulnerability detection and exploit development capabilities. OpenAI also said the model is more reliable at staying within the authorised boundaries of security testing, reducing the risk of it targeting systems outside a researcher’s scope.GPT-6 Cyber shows major improvement in security testsOpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber scored 48.5% on ExploitGym, a benchmark that tests whether AI models can exploit specified vulnerabilities in remote targets. This is up from 32.1% for GPT-5.6 Cyber, marking a 51% relative improvement. The model also performed better in web penetration testing, achieving 40.3% recall of vulnerabilities compared with 32% for GPT-6 Astra.In a separate evaluation designed to test whether AI agents follow security testing boundaries, GPT-6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases without deployment safety prompts. With the prompts enabled, it stayed within scope in 100% of tests.OpenAI has classified GPT-6 Cyber as “Critical” in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, compared with the “High” rating assigned to GPT-5.6 Cyber.GPT-6 Cyber finds vulnerabilities in Linux and FirefoxOpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 Linux kernel vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948 of them. The company disclosed 304 critical findings to Linux maintainers with candidate patches, while work to fix other vulnerabilities is ongoing. The model also identified 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox. OpenAI shared reproducible tests and proposed patches with Mozilla, which has released fixes for many of the issues. The research also found that 30 previously known Firefox vulnerabilities were more severe than earlier assessments suggested.Security teams at companies including Cisco, Calif and CodeRabbit are using GPT-6 Cyber for vulnerability research and code review. OpenAI has also used the model to identify and fix weaknesses in its own infrastructure.GPT-6 Cyber accessOpenAI said GPT-6 Cyber is initially available through its API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. The company plans to expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon.It is also strengthening safeguards to prevent misuse, including monitoring for unauthorised cyber activity and protections against high-risk assistance involving critical infrastructure such as power plants and water treatment facilities. OpenAI said organisations and individual security researchers can apply for its Daybreak programme to access cybersecurity tools and resources.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: At least 10 local governments have moved to drop Flock’s surveillance cameras since summer | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The concerns range from privacy to how data is shared (and with whom) to procurement concerns.
articles.body:
At least 10 local governments and police departments have moved since this summer to curb, restrict, or end their use of Flock Safety technology as concerns about mass surveillance and data privacy continue to grow . The backlash is part of a broader pushback against the rapid adoption of advanced AI technology, including the data center buildout, facial recognition, and other uses of AI.

Flock, founded in 2017, sells surveillance software — like license plate readers, drones, and microphone-based edge-computing devices to pick up gunshots and other sounds — that can help solve crimes, such as finding missing people or stolen cars. More than 100,000 Flock cameras are in use nationwide.

But in the past three months, Monroe , Ohio; Newburgh , New York; Richmond , Virginia; Hopkinton, Massachusetts; New Bedford , Massachusetts; and Lansing , Michigan, have all moved to end their contracts with Flock. Meanwhile, police in East Bridgewater and Grafton, Massachusetts, also announced plans to stop using Flock cameras. Just this week, residents of League City, Texas, voted against their police department’s continued use of Flock’s license plate readers, and the cameras are now set to be removed.

The concerns range from privacy to how data is shared (and with whom) to procurement concerns.

In Asheville, North Carolina, police lost access to Flock after the city voted to terminate its contract in August, and the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office in Colorado announced in September that it would stop using Flock cameras. When asked for comment, the El Paso County Sheriff’s Office redirected TechCrunch to its press release, where Sheriff Joseph Roybal said that discontinuing the use of Flock was the right decision for the county.

“We have the tools, training, and experience to locate and apprehend criminals without relying on Flock cameras,” he said in the press release.

Tatiana Rice, a senior director for U.S. legislation at The Future of Privacy Forum, told TechCrunch that the backlash to Flock isn’t surprising and only further represents the “growing public skepticism toward technology.” Flock is a target because people can see the sensors and cameras as they drive along roads; data centers have also become physical embodiments of the resentment growing against emerging technology. “A camera at the end of your street is tangible in a way that everyday sharing and selling of personal data online is not,” Rice said.

At the state level this summer, for example, Florida barred license plate readers from state highways, while Texas paused state funding for Flock. The issues again range from data privacy concerns to misuse of the technology.

Misuse has been a real problem. In August, for example, an officer in Brentwood, Missouri was accused of using Flock cameras to stalk his ex-wife during their divorce. In September, an officer from East Texas was sentenced to prison for using Flock to stalk his ex-girlfriend and her family.

Another growing concern is how immigration officials have been able to access the technology. One case that captures the issue came in March, when Ithaca, New York, passed a resolution to terminate its contract with the Flock Group.

In the resolution, the city said there were “proven instances of Flock Safety infrastructure being used by federal agents for information purposes even without specific authorizations from the contracting locality,” and that the city had reviewed reports that “either intentionally or through its negligence,” Flock had allowed U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to “use query results from its database of state and local ALPR [automatic license plate reader] data to investigate and persecute immigrants throughout the United States.”

“Every day, police departments across the country are using Flock technology to solve serious crimes, locate suspects, find missing people, and make a measurable impact on public safety,” Flock told TechCrunch in a statement. “While we respect every community’s decision, removing a tool that is actively helping solve violent crimes and protect communities moves public safety backward. Every Flock customer owns its data and controls who it is shared with and how it can be used. Flock does not sell data and does not have a contract with ICE.”

This August, Flock announced it would shorten the default period it stores data for new customers, from 30 days to seven. It also said agencies now need a case code before they can search the database.

The conversation around Flock echoes, in many ways, the fight over data centers. Many of these cities adopted Flock just a few years ago, and residents likely had no idea it was being installed, Adam Schwartz of the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a digital privacy nonprofit that has investigated Flock before, told TechCrunch.

That lack of awareness is similar to how data centers are popping up across the country, often before residents understand what is happening. Schwartz said police departments often decide to use Flock on their own, with little oversight from city councils. In South Windsor , Connecticut, according to local reports, Flock cameras went live last year without public warning or a vote. In October, the town voted to remove its Flock cameras.

“Grassroots activists across the country have been demanding that city councils exercise their procurement power to refuse to pay for ALPRs,” Schwartz said, referring to councils’ power to decide what the city buys. He added that activists have been fighting for years and that “many city councils are listening.”

The main argument for technology like Flock is that it helps combat crime and keep neighborhoods safe. And many local governments are not dropping Flock or similar technology; instead, they are adding restrictions on its use or looking for alternatives.

Cleveland, Ohio, for example, voted this summer to extend its contract with Flock, but has started restricting searches related to immigration. It has also limited access to the database to the Cleveland Police alone, cutting off the Northeast Ohio Regional Fusion Center, essentially a federal intelligence agency, which had initially been given access.

“They are used and needed for investigative purposes,” the city said when reached for comment. “The Department of Public Safety is currently reviewing responses to an RFP [request for proposals] that was sent out to other vendors that provide the same technology as Flock.”

But as with data centers, communities want more say in the trade-offs. “These tools can offer real public safety benefits, but communities are clearly interested in ensuring that those benefits are not at the cost of their civil liberties,” Rice said. Surveillance technology will likely remain a political hot topic, especially since Democrats now control Congress.

In September, President Donald Trump said he liked Flock’s technology “because of law enforcement,” even though a Reuters poll that same month found that more Americans dislike the technology than like it.

Also that month, Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican from Kentucky, introduced a bill called the Flock-Off Act to bar the use of federal money to buy “ Flock-style surveillance ” and put other safeguards in place. In October, Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.), Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), and Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) introduced the Ban Flock Act to end “the rise of AI-powered surveillance cameras.”

articles.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data center site in Amsterdam
articles.summary: Europe is witnessing a wave of protests against data centers.
articles.body: Protesters have broken into a construction site of a new Microsoft data center in Amsterdam this morning. Members of the Geef Tegengas group helped organize the protest against the construction of three 85-meter data center towers in the outskirts of Amsterdam. Reuters reports that around 100 people made it into the construction site, with some scaling a crane to place a “fuck AI” banner. Protesters also unfurled a “Microsoft powers genocide” banner on the construction site, and chanted “Microsoft has got to go” and “free Palestine.” Opposition to the new data center in Amsterdam comes more than a year after the city banned new data centers until 2030, after a temporary stop that was announced at the end of 2023. Microsoft will be the sole tenant of this new data center, and the project is proceeding as it was planned as far back as 2016, before a ban was put in place. The site, being built by British developer Pure Data Centres, has also managed to navigate some loopholes to reach the construction stage. The protests over Microsoft’s data center site in Amsterdam comes in the same week that activists staged a mock Israeli military checkpoint outside a Microsoft data center in Dublin on Tuesday, part of a wave of data center protests across Europe. Earlier this week, voters across the US also rejected unrestrained development of data centers. AI data centers are continuing to pop up across the US, with frequent opposition from locals concerned about the impact on their communities. Microsoft also abandoned the UK’s largest data center project last month, after local electricity grid officials said the site won’t be supplied with power until the 2030s. The software maker has also faced a wave of protests from former employees over the past year. Microsoft’s 50th anniversary party was interrupted by employees protesting the use of Microsoft’s technologies in Israel’s war against Hamas, with one calling Microsoft’s AI CEO, Mustafa Suleyman, a “war profiteer.“ A Microsoft employee also disrupted the company’s Build developer conference last year, interrupting Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella’s keynote. Months later, Microsoft fired two employee protesters who occupied its president’s office.

articles.title: Underdog shows off a 32MB speech model in new demo
articles.summary: Despite its small size, Underdog's new model can generate both speech and music.
articles.body:
AI companies across the world are racing to make bigger and better models, but the problem is all of them need massive amounts of processing power. On the other end, some researchers and startups are creating smaller models that can run on edge devices, like your phone or computer.

One such startup, Underdog, has released a game built with its new voice model called Woof that’s only 32MB large.

The game features a room with a retro tech theme, a typewriter, and a CRT monitor. There is a desk lamp, which makes a sound when you click its switch. The intro warns users about “intrusive” cloud providers in the town — ostensibly a jab at cloud-based models.

You can interact with the typewriter and music tuner.

You can type anything on the typewriter using your keyboard, and the game will speak it back. You can also rotate the tuner to generate different kinds of music.

All of this works within the browser through Underdog’s speech generation model, which, the company says, can run on most devices without any internet connection. The model has 31 million parameters and is open for everyone to download.

While such a small model likely won’t replace bigger models, it may still be enough to drive local assistant experiences or create personalized podcasts.

This demo comes weeks after Underdog launched Bark , a 167 MB speech-to-text model also designed to run on edge devices for transcription and dictation.

Sigil Wen, the founder of Underdog , told TechCrunch that he started building the app because, instead of using notetakers like Granola, he wanted to build his own system with AI models that can run on users’ devices and let them own their data.

“I think we will be able to run most capable models of today on the devices you already own within months. We just want to train the best open models that are American-made, that are open, that are capable and allow people to have private AI,” he said, referring to his manifesto .

In addition to the two voice models mentioned above, Underdog has also released a 27-billion-parameter model that can run on laptops, along with a waitlisted app that the company is positioning as a locally-hosted alternative to Muse and Instinct.

articles.title: Strategist Who Warned Before Rout Sees Anthropic as Bigger Risk
articles.summary: One of the few Wall Street strategists to turn cautious on stocks ahead of Thursday’s selloff warned that a potential Anthropic PBC debut may prove a more de...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- One of the few Wall Street strategists to turn cautious on stocks ahead of Thursday's selloff warned that a potential Anthropic PBC debut may prove a more decisive event than the US midterms.

HSBC Holdings Plc's Max Kettner cut his rating on stocks from maximum overweight to neutral two weeks ago, arguing that the narrative around tech had turned unfavorable regardless of how companies approached capital spending.

While he sees the artificial intelligence trade as fundamentally intact despite this week's heavy selling, he remains cautious after the vote, questioning how much risk could have cleared when investors had done little to hedge the election in the first place.

"The real risk clearing event is probably the Anthropic IPO in two weeks, if it happens. The best case would probably be you come, but you come with a $1 trillion valuation instead of $1.5 trillion valuation," he said.

Anthropic's planned initial public offering faces various hurdles. Recent selling in AI-related stocks has made the market backdrop less forgiving, while a changing of the guard in Washington also risks shifting expectations for Anthropic's ability to navigate the political landscape.

"You come with a reasonably low valuation, such that in the secondary market you actually start rallying. Or at least not dumping 20-30% in the first week — because that obviously would be horrible."

Kettner made a name for himself in recent years as one of the first to call the current bull run in stocks. But last month he cut back on his bet on stocks for the first time in months. He argued that sharp mood changes among investors warranted a more cautious approach ahead of the US midterms.

"Wednesday was really strange," he told Bloomberg, referring to the initial post-vote rally. "People were asking me, 'Why are you still cautious? Why are you still on the sidelines? What are you doing?'"

For Kettner, the explanations for the rally and then the sharp fall Thursday felt more like narratives being retrofitted to the price action that had genuinely surprised investors. The S&P 500 had its worst day since April 2025, while the Nasdaq 100 and chip index suffered their steepest declines since March 2020.
