articles.title: Meta's former security chief Alex Stamos says giving Muse AI your passwords and finances is "totally insane"
articles.summary: Alex Stamos is warning against giving AI agents access to your passwords and financial information.
articles.body:
The former security chief of Meta is warning people about the access they might be giving the company's Muse AI agent without considering the consequences.

Alex Stamos, appearing on an episode of the "Big Technology Podcast " on Oct. 23, said it was "totally insane" that people are giving AI agent apps, including Muse, access to personal data such as their finances and other sensitive information.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

Of particular concern to Stamos was AI gaining access to people's password vaults, which gives it broad access to all corners of their lives.

"People using agents and then being like, 'Hey, … Muse, here's my entire 1Password. Go handle my finances for me. Go file my taxes' is totally insane," said Stamos.

Meta did not immediately reply to a Moneywise request for comment about Stamos' statements, but on its website , the company said it believed Muse to be safe , since it runs on a virtual machine that Meta said is "isolated so no one else's agent can access it."

However, the company added, "no automated system is perfect," so users should "review Muse's activity and only grant the access you're comfortable with."

Stamos, who is now chief security officer for the AI coding startup Cognition, also pointed to Spear Street Technology's Instinct as an AI tool that users are giving access to. Doing so and instructing the tool to handle your finances for you puts banks in an awkward position, he said.

"So [banks] … now see all of these interactions with them that are authenticated correctly — so they're not stolen credentials — but are clearly bots doing interaction," Stamos said.

Some banks have issued warnings about this practice — and even blocked AI agents from accessing accounts. According to CNBC , JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has said the bank currently blocks external AI agents from operating on customers' behalf.

On the company's earnings call in October, Dimon said , "If people are using them, they should understand the risk. There's a liability transfer. They should understand there's a liability transfer. If data is being misused, they should understand it's being misused."

articles.title: Amazon will let you text Alexa your shopping list
articles.summary: Amazon is adding a new feature to Alexa for Shopping that allows customers to purchase items by texting the AI shopping assistant.﻿
articles.body: Amazon is adding a new feature to Alexa for Shopping that allows customers to purchase items by texting the AI shopping assistant. Users can describe the products they’re looking to buy and/or provide a photograph of the item, and Alexa for Shopping will search for matching results in Amazon listings, text back with recommendations, and order the item on the users’ behalf. This launch builds on the existing Alexa for Shopping experience that launched in May, allowing users to place orders during moments where texting is more convenient than using Amazon’s app or website. The contact will appear in your phone as “Amazon Alexa,” and can be used for a wide range of shopping requests, including ordering weekly groceries, asking for gift recommendations, finding similar products to something you’ve snapped a photo of, and more. Alexa says it remembers your personal preferences over time (so if you frequently ask for vegan options, it’ll bear that in mind for product recommendations), and can track deals and prices to text you when an item you’re watching has gone on sale. The texting capability is rolling out to a small group of Amazon customers in the US starting today, who will receive a text message inviting them to try the experience. It will then roll out to “millions more customers” in the coming weeks, according to Amazon’s announcement. [Image: At least this example shows you an image of the product before asking if you’re happy to buy it. “Customers often jot down what they need the moment they think of it in their notes, in their messages, in their group chats,” said Rajiv Mehta, vice president of Conversational Shopping at Amazon. “Now with Alexa for Shopping, your personal shopping agent is just a text away. Message it what you need and Alexa goes to work on your behalf — searching, comparing, and buying so you can get on with your day.” Amazon is one of several companies that have introduced ways to text their chatbots. Last month saw OpenAI launching a feature that allows users to exchange text messages with its personal AI agent, Dot. DoorDash also introduced a text-based ordering feature in September that lets users get dish recommendations and order food by texting the Ask DoorDash AI chatbot.

articles.title: After blocking Muse, Amazon now lets users text Alexa to help them shop | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Amazon said that the feature will roll out to millions of users in coming weeks.
articles.body:
Amazon is jumping on the currently most popular bandwagon for interacting with AI agents: texting. The company on Friday said it is launching a feature that lets customers chat with its Alexa AI agent over text messages to help them shop, much like you can with AI agents like Muse or Instinct.

The move comes after Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse from querying its site in September. The company is rolling the features out just before the start of the holiday shopping season.

The e-commerce giant said select U.S. customers will get a text asking them to enable the shopping feature. Those with access can text Alexa to shop on Amazon using natural language queries, spanning everything from searching for items, adding them to cart, and purchasing.

The text agent builds on the recent shopping-focused upgrades to Alexa , and so can manage lists, keep tabs on prices, search for items across the web, compare products, and check the status of orders. Users can also share a picture of an item or someone wearing an outfit to search for similar listings on Amazon.

The company said over time, Alexa will learn users’ preferences and suggest items accordingly.

The company said users who don’t get invited to use this feature can sign up to a waitlist . The feature will be rolled out more broadly in the coming weeks.

As the market for consumer-focused AI agents balloons, platforms like Amazon are building their own to tap this new avenue of user interaction. Last month, delivery company DoorDash said that third-party agents had so far only placed hundreds of orders in total on its platform, and that it plans to concentrate on developing its own text-based agent, launched in September , further.

articles.title: Anthropic's IPO valuation could plunge to near $1 trillion amid market turmoil
articles.summary: Anthropic's IPO valuation plunges as markets whipsaw.
articles.body:
Yesterday's bruising market sell-off sent tech stocks plunging on questions about what the newly elected Democratic majority in Congress means for the data center build-out and AI.

The pain was so acute it's bled into Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) upcoming IPO. According to Bloomberg and The Wall Street Journal , investors are now eyeing a potential market valuation of between $1 trillion and $1.3 trillion for the AI startup.

That's far below the $ 2 trillion buyers were projecting just last month when stocks were flying high.

Anthropic, which publicly filed its S-1 investor prospectus last Monday and updated it this week with more recent revenue and spending numbers , is widely expected to launch its IPO sometime before the end of the month.

But that could slip to a later date due to the broader market sell-off.

Odds that the AI lab goes public before Dec. 1 have plummeted on prediction markets Polymarket and Kalshi, dropping from roughly 80% to near 50%.

Tuesday's election results are seen as a broad repudiation of the AI movement and data center construction across the country, as voters registered anxieties about potential job displacement and the impact of data centers on local communities.

That has raised concerns about the nationwide data center build-out, which became a flashpoint in the lead-up to the election, with President Trump widely supporting the effort.

Democrats, and some Republicans, however, seized on backlash against data centers and AI more broadly, driving concerns that projects could be canceled or otherwise hindered.

Meta ( META ) president Dina Powell McCormick told an audience at the Wall Street Journal's WSJ Tech event on Wednesday that building data centers will be harder following the election results.

On Thursday, OpenAI ( OPAI.PVT ) outlined its latest policy proposals for data centers it owns and operates, including ending non-disclosure agreements with towns and paying the full cost of the electricity it uses and the infrastructure needed to serve the company's facilities.

The Anthropic rival was initially expected to go public by the end of the year, but pushed that out to early 2027.

And while that was originally seen as a potential sign of weakness for OpenAI's public debut, given the current market volatility, it may end up working in the company's favor.

articles.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: AI usage keeps climbing, but spending has stalled. Price cuts and smarter cost controls among the biggest spenders could challenge investor assumptions about AI hypergrowth.
articles.body:
Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.

As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.

Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Khazarian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”

“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.

October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Khazarian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Khazarian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.

Khazarian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Khazarian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.

“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Khazarian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.

“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Khazarian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”

The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.

“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Khazarian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”

Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brr. Costs go ahhh.”

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Khazarian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.

Khazarian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Khazarian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Khazarian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

articles.title: AI is the new dating dealbreaker
articles.summary: Swipe left if you’re not aligned.
articles.body: When Irene moved to San Francisco last year, she started using dating apps as a way to meet new people, get to know her new city, and connect with others who care about the things she does. After the 25-year-old analyst downloaded Hinge and started swiping, she noticed a trend. “Hinge has a prompt where you can say, ‘We’ll get along if”,” she recalls. “Sometimes people will be like, ‘Fuck AI.’” Usually, the people who include this kind of value statement on their profile work in the arts, nursing, maybe graphic design. Within the span of a few minutes of sitting down and swiping, Irene shows me a second profile where this happened once more: “You should *not* go out with me if… you use AI.” In San Francisco, the epicenter of tech, the metaphorical AI bomb went off in 2022 with the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT. Conversations surrounding artificial intelligence now permeate the dating scene in one shape or another. Over the past month, I bopped around the city, chatting with people at parties and coworking spaces and reviewing dating directories and other online profiles, trying to find out how AI affects the dating scene. Responses varied wildly. For some, AI feelings take on a similar valence to traditionally political ones, showing up in dating profiles next to party affiliation or other signifiers, like the watermelon emoji symbolizing solidarity with Palestinians amid the war in Gaza. Others are wrestling with the ethics of dating someone who builds AI, considering the financial benefits a partner in the industry can bring, weighing whether to have children in a future this uncertain, or even handing their love lives over to it entirely. On a street near Berkeley, I meet up with Kyle. (His name has been changed so that he can talk openly about his personal life.) Kyle is a researcher at an AI safety nonprofit initiative, and although he is just in his early 20s, he’s already thinking about death. In the AI safety community, some experts see a 10 percent chance of humans going extinct due to AI taking over. This apocalyptic possibility is always top of mind when he navigates conversations with a potential partner: The rapid development of AI shapes how he thinks about whether he wants to have kids or where he might live long term — if there is even a long term. “A lot of people are planning for what they want their life to look like five, 10, 15 years down the line,” Kyle says, raising his gaze and looking off into the distance. Life could change depending on whether the world manages to get AI alignment right, he tells me. “For me, it’s hard to have that planning conversation because I don’t really expect a long-term future,” he says. He tries to have these conversations in person rather than over text, so a date can ask follow-up questions about why he sees the future the way he does. For now, he’s focusing on finding a partner with whom he enjoys spending time. When I ask Kyle if he would date someone who works in artificial intelligence or tech, he says that he would have to think hard about it. He believes that a lot of people who work at frontier AI companies are doing things that he considers pretty heinous. “They don’t think very hard about the societal impacts of their actions because they’re mostly in it for the paycheck or because it’s interesting,” he says. But Bryan, who works at a frontier AI company and also asked to go by a pseudonym, doesn’t believe that feelings about AI matter when it comes to romance. “I just don’t think it’s a factor at all. Like, it’s the least [relevant] thing,” says Bryan, who recently started a relationship. To him, dating is more about weighing a series of factors: how someone talks and approaches problems, how they have fun. Despite his day job (and whatever someone like Kyle might think of him for it), he believes that working out more and looking better probably increases someone’s chances of getting a match way more than any AI or non-AI affiliation. But, he says, “The one way it interacts is that there are a bunch of people who are rich from AI, and, you know, being wealthy is always a plus.” Bryan isn’t exactly wrong about the benefits of a high-paying job in AI. With the IPOs of Anthropic and OpenAI in the next year, matchmakers have found that clients are specifying “AI engineer” on their list of preferred dating profile qualifications. And stability is particularly attractive right now: According to a CBRE report released in August, more than 20,000 AI jobs were added to the San Francisco Bay Area’s technology workforce, even as overall tech talent contracted by 6 percent since 2022. “Member of technical staff” roles have become very lucrative jobs; the average salary of an AI researcher can be around $300,000. According to the New York Post, one matchmaker found that her client booked a six-month stay in San Francisco because of the possibility of meeting a significant other who might be connected to an AI company going through an IPO. AI is reflected in the way the technology is seeping into San Franciscans’ everyday habits — including those that shape relationships, from how people process their feelings to whom they confide in. Andromeda, who works as an EMT and a registered behavior technician as well as an AI security analyst, says she’s worried about the unintended consequences of talking to AI chatbots, especially for questions about (and possibly the replacement of) human connection. According to a study released by Elon University, 27 percent of Americans are turning to AI chatbots with personal, emotional, or social queries. Thirty-eight percent of the surveyed group said they occasionally tell AI things that they would not tell other people, including their romantic partners. Andromeda weighs the pros and cons of dating someone who would use bots for “emotional regulation.” “Socially and psychologically, it’s a big deal, and we have to talk about it,” she says. She appreciates the role that a chatbot can play to help someone better express themselves. “I would certainly date a man who uses AI to talk through intense thoughts and feelings and to brainstorm clarity.” At the same time, she is also reluctant to date someone who might abuse a chatbot, since it’s maladaptive behavior and does not represent good values for model welfare. “If they treat ChatGPT badly today, it will be me tomorrow!” If Andromeda worries about what people tell chatbots, others have gone a step further and let AI do the talking for them. At the Hugging Face Open Source Week party, Joseph, a 21-year-old software engineer, explains how he has automated his dating life. Working 14 hours a day to launch his startup, he has decided to outsource swiping on Hinge entirely to an AI agent. The agent is managed by his human virtual assistant from the Philippines and has been fine-tuned to mimic the way that he speaks and acts. Looking at each profile, the AI agent sends tailored outreach messages to spark a conversation. After some back and forth, the agent determines if the woman is compatible with Joseph and, if so, books open slots on his weekend calendars for dating in person. “If you are a founder, you have to put a value on your time, so you can’t be doing low-leverage activities. Protect your dopamine, folks,” Joseph tells me at The Midway in San Francisco’s Dogpatch district, where hundreds don white bucket hats and dance next to Hugging Face’s round, foam emoji mascot. “It’s kind of a copy-and-paste sequence that happens with every girl to get to know about you, understand your backstory, and so on and so forth.” He’s not alone. A 2025 survey by Match and the Kinsey Institute found that 26 percent of singles in the United States use AI tools to enhance their dating experiences. Hinge now has an AI tool to generate suggested responses, and Bumble will soon phase out swiping in favor of AI assistant-facilitated matchmaking. Joseph says he won’t share the secret sauce of his AI agent on GitHub, but he tells me it’s pretty easy to make one on Claude Code. “It has been extremely successful. I’m averaging two closed conversions a week,” he says, meaning that he goes on two dates with two different people. The women on the other side don’t know. The point is to meet in real life. The overall process has lowered what he calls “CPN,” or “cost per nut.” At 29 years old, JJ has stopped using dating apps. Instead, she turns to the Date-Me Directory — a collection of longform, resume-like documents where people write personal dating profiles — to find a partner. Two years ago, she worked in product design in New York, but she transitioned into the AI safety field because she felt that it aligned more with her effective altruist morals. Upon reviewing troves of Date-Me Docs for the San Francisco / Berkeley area, I noticed that quite a few people mention “the singularity” as a factor of whether to have kids. The so-called “singularity” is the point of when technology overtakes human control; some have pointed to the development of true artificial general intelligence as the point of no return. According to JJ, many people in AI safety specifically use the Date-Me Docs as a way to meet people. “Don’t want kids in the pre-singularity future, if there’s a post-singularity future then I might want kids then,” one document states. On the other hand, similar to climate doom anxieties, other people are looking at whether having children is ethical amid massive structural changes in society caused by AI. “Is the world good, getting to a good place, or is it bad? And if it’s good, baby. If not, no baby, because you’re gonna bring a baby into a world full of potential suffering,” JJ says, explaining the train of thought that these Date-Me Doc potential suitors might have. She does not consider herself a doomer, but she is still pressed for her own singularity timeline. (2029, she suspects.) If anything, she jokes that the approaching end times makes her more likely to want a baby around: “If the bomb gets me, I want to be holding a shiny child.” These existential concerns have translated into a backlash against tech, San Francisco included. “Stop the AI” rallies have spread to events like Salesforce’s Dreamforce convention and OpenAI’s DevDay, with protestors calling out tech companies and their roles in data center development and ICE raids. That skepticism has spilled into how people size up a potential match, even at local events designed to bring the Bay Area together. At a pop-up “Date My Friend” pitch event at the Kilowatt Bar in the Mission District on a Saturday evening, a dozen people pitched their friends and exes to a crowd of more than a hundred. “He works in tech, but he’s unhappy about it,” one person announced to a chorus of cheers. Other people cracked jokes that their PowerPoints were clearly made by humans, not AI. Annalise Wulf, 26, one of the three cofounders of the “Date My Friend” series, says that although people in San Francisco try to “tech maxx” their lives, more tech workers with crazy schedules are interested in analog, in-person events to go back to the roots of meeting and creating community. “It’s like, ‘I’m here because I’m not using an AI dating app right now. Like I’m trying to do something different,’” Wulf says. “I do think it’s maybe popular now to be more anti-tech,” says Lucy Segraves, 28, one of the other cofounders. If someone is working for a company that people see as perpetuating war crimes through their technology, she might be more hesitant to date them. But ultimately, she says, there are more immediate concerns. “As a person with a non-tech job, I never judge someone if they do work in tech,” Lucy says. “Because that’s unfortunately where the money is, and we’re all just trying to make it in life.”

articles.title: Microsoft Is Winding Down Oracle Deal to Rent AI Cloud Capacity
articles.summary: Microsoft Corp. is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle Corp., part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partners...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Microsoft Corp. is winding down an arrangement to rent AI computing from Oracle Corp., part of a larger reassessment of billions of dollars in cloud partnerships.

In recent months, Microsoft has been turning off rented computing capacity from Oracle after declining to renew the contract, according to people familiar with the matter.

Over time, the computing Microsoft was renting became less useful because it no longer fit the company's specifications, said the people, who requested anonymity to discuss a private matter. The Oracle hardware used older-generation Nvidia Corp. chips, the people said.

An Oracle spokesperson said demand for the company's AI infrastructure remains strong, including for earlier-generation graphics processing units. Oracle said in September that it was renewing contracts for four-year-old GPUs at a 20% premium to the original deal price.

Under the arrangement, announced in 2023, Oracle agreed to sell Microsoft access to servers that would power a new AI-assisted version of the Bing search engine. The full size of the deal couldn't be determined.

The fact that Microsoft was prepared to rent servers from a major rival was seen as an early indication of the massive shortage of processing power that has come to define the AI era.

The world's largest software maker helped usher in a "neocloud" boom by signing massive contracts with upstart cloud businesses like CoreWeave, Nscale and Nebius. In all, Microsoft committed more than $80 billion to rent capacity from other cloud companies to bolster its own AI efforts.

But Microsoft has been re-thinking its strategy. Key leaders at the company have grown frustrated with the neocloud providers over high costs and delays. In recent months, the company has tightened oversight of data center projects, stepped away from ones it deems risky and debated internally whether to ink new neocloud deals, Bloomberg previously reported.

Oracle's cloud businesses has expanded rapidly since 2023, fueled by big AI contracts with companies like OpenAI and Meta Platforms Inc. For the year that ended in May 2026, Oracle's cloud business posted $18 billion in revenue.

articles.title: Meta introduces Spaces, a new way to collaborate with your Muse agent | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Meta's Muse agents continue to get new features and integrations. Spaces promises to be a new way to interact with the AI helpers.
articles.body:
Meta recently launched its Muse agents — a new generation of cuddly agentic helpers. Now, the company has launched Spaces, a new way to communicate and collaborate with them.

As far as I can tell, Spaces are basically breakout conversations that revolve around a particular topic — although Meta refers to them as “custom experiences.” They live in the sidebar of the interface where you interact with your Muse agent. Clicking on the Space brings up the conversation, where Muse works toward a particular goal on your behalf.

For instance, if you wanted to plan a vacation, you could open a new Space focused on that particular project, and whenever you want to work on it with Muse, you would click to open that particular tab. Or, if you’re focused on collecting recipes for an upcoming family event, you’d open a new Space for that particular project. Other examples Meta gives are a holiday gift tracker, a wedding planner, or a space for DIY projects.

“Describe an idea in chat, and Muse builds a space for you, whether that’s a tracker, a planner or a project board,” Meta says.

Spaces can also be easily integrated with third-party apps and information, Meta says.

“Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask,” the company says.

On Friday, Mark Zuckerberg, Meta’s founder and CEO, posted about the new feature on X: “Playing around with spaces in Muse lately — tell Muse what you need and it builds it. I’ve made a BBQ game, an event tracker, and a home control dashboard. Excited to see what you build.”

Muse agents — and the cuddly avatars that enclose them — have been greeted with a relatively warm reception over the past few months. During its earnings call in October, Zuckerberg said that its agents had 10 million users in the U.S. and Canada — less than two months after the agents debuted.

The company is obviously busy building out the user experience around the agents. Spaces is actually the second new Muse feature that Meta has debuted over the last week. On Thursday, the company also announced Muse Voice , which allows users to video chat with their agent and give it commands verbally.

The company is in competition with other cute and cuddly AI agents — including OpenAI’s dots and SpaceXAI’s Grokbot , which were debuted with similarly cartoonish personas.

articles.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation | TechCrunch
articles.summary: OpenAI has reportedly raised an additional $11 billion as part of a funding round that hasn't closed yet but is expected to in the coming weeks.
articles.body:
OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter. The $11 billion is part of a larger funding round that hasn’t closed yet, according to the outlet. The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.

In late September, Bloomberg reported that OpenAI was looking to raise $30 billion in the upcoming round. The current figures fall well short of that target.

TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted. Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.

OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans. There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

The market for AI hangs in a particularly precarious place. The Democratic landslide in the U.S. midterms — and overwhelmingly negative voter sentiment around data centers — has caused jitters throughout the market , with many anticipating potential regulatory challenges in the future.

articles.title: China reportedly recruited AI exec to spy on Jensen Huang
articles.summary: China’s intelligence agency recruited a businesswoman, Alice Huang, to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times.
articles.body: China’s intelligence agency recruited Megaspeed executive Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to The New York Times. The Ministry of State Security (MSS) enlisted her to glean information about American AI chips and “potentially influence the company to push for its most advanced chips to be made available to China.” Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia’s, and Alice Huang also has “relationships with executives at the highest levels of the A.I. chip industry,” including leaders at Gigabyte, the NYT says. Last week, the NYT reported that Jensen Huang was seen as the target of a “Chinese spy plot” and shared details about Alice Huang and Jensen Huang’s relationship, but the information that China’s MSS had recruited her is new. The NYT describes the relationship between Alice Huang and Jensen Huang, who are not related, as “close.” President Trump, who is friendly with Jensen Huang, was briefed last year about the relationship, but didn’t take any action. Yesterday, three House committees asked Jensen Huang to appear for a joint, closed-door briefing on his “interactions” with Alice Huang.

articles.body: OpenAI is now valued at $1.25 trillion in a new round of funding that has raised another $11 billion, according to Bloomberg. Echoing FT and Wall Street Journal reports from last week, Bloomberg says OpenAI is still pursuing additional investments that could increase the amount to $20 billion, and that it had initially hoped to raise as much as $30 billion at a higher valuation of $1.4 trillion. That was before tech stocks dropped, and the results of the midterms showed how much public opinion has turned against AI companies and data center projects. OpenAI’s rival Anthropic filed its S-1 to go public last week. He didn’t give a specific timeline for the IPO, but said at the time, “I think it’s also kind of bad for the world if OpenAI waits too long to go public.”

articles.title: US Believes Woman Close to Nvidia CEO Was a China Spy, NYT Says
articles.summary: US intelligence officials told the Trump administration that a woman who had become close to Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was working fo...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- US intelligence officials told the Trump administration that a woman who had become close to Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was working for a Chinese spy agency, which recruited her to collect information on him, the New York Times reported Friday.

The newspaper cited unnamed sources who it said had been told of American surveillance conducted on the woman, Alice Huang, an executive with an Asian technology company called Megaspeed International. Administration officials learned of the accusations in an intelligence memo, the Times said.

Alice Huang was working for Beijing's Ministry of State Security, which was maneuvering to glean more detail about American artificial intelligence chips, according to the Times, and possibly persuade Nvidia to try to make its most sophisticated semiconductors available to the Chinese.

It was not clear when or how she met Jensen Huang.

Earlier: Nvidia CEO Pressed by US Lawmakers Over Tie to Firm in Spy Probe

The case has taken on new urgency following this week's US midterm elections, which will give Democrats control of Congress. Republicans also are scrutinizing Huang's ties to the alleged spy.

The House Select Committee on China said in a statement on Thursday that it had sent a letter to Jensen Huang "requesting his participation in a joint, closed-door briefing."

"The letter details the lawmakers' concerns regarding Huang's interactions with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset, and the company's security protocols against foreign adversary espionage," the panel said in the statement.

Megaspeed is part of Nvidia's cloud partner network. The Singapore-based company buys equipment from the chipmaker and rents out computing power to AI developers.

Nvidia said in a statement after the Times article was published that its cloud partners "do not ask us to seek changes in US law or advocate for sales to China." The company added that "anyone seeking classified information through our NCP customers would have hit a dead end. We neither have nor share classified information with customers."

The Central Intelligence Agency and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday evening.

articles.title: Crusoe sells troubled Wyoming data center project to Google
articles.summary: The deal highlights the challenges of developing massive AI data centers.
articles.body:
Crusoe, an eight-year-old, Denver-based data center developer recently valued at $30.9 billion , confirmed Friday it has sold an unfinished data center project in southeastern Wyoming to Google.

Google, which Crusoe had tried and failed to land as a customer for the project, is taking over the development after reportedly raising concerns about its cost and construction timeline under Crusoe’s management.

Crusoe initially announced the project last year with Blackstone-backed infrastructure company Tallgrass, planning to eventually scale it to 10 gigawatts of power capacity.

Google did not disclose how much it paid Crusoe for the unfinished project, bu it announced plans to invest $17 billion to develop the data center campus.

The deal highlights how difficult it can be for independent data center developers to deliver massive projects on time and within budget, given the challenges of securing equipment and power. Growing opposition from local communities can further complicate development.

Despite taking over the Wyoming facility, Google hasn’t walked away from working with Crusoe entirely. Crusoe is developing another data center for Google near Amarillo, Texas.

The deal to sell the site to Google was first reported by Bloomberg in June, but the Wyoming setback didn’t stop Crusoe from raising a $3.9 billion round in September.

Crusoe makes money by leasing data center space to customers that bring their own GPUs, by renting out its own GPUs, and by selling compute power used to run AI models, known as inference.

Crusoe’s largest projects serve some of the biggest names in AI. Its campus in Abilene, Texas, is being built in phases for Oracle and OpenAI, and the company is also constructing a separate 900-megawatt campus next door for Microsoft, with its first building expected to come online in mid-2027. Meta is also a customer, and Bloomberg reported that the trading firm Jane Street signed a $13 billion , five-year cloud deal with Crusoe.

Crusoe was founded by Chase Lochmiller, now its CEO, and Cully Cavness, who started it as a cryptocurrency-mining business powered by natural gas that would otherwise have been burned off. In September, alongside its $3.9 billion funding round, the company added three board members , including JB Straubel, the Redwood Materials founder and Tesla board member who invested in Crusoe in 2021. Crusoe later became the first customer of Straubel’s energy-storage business.

articles.title: From the front row to the hot seat — what the midterms mean for Big Tech | TechCrunch
articles.summary: After spending two years getting cozy with the White House, Big Tech is suddenly trying to make friends with Democrats, and the open question is whether that image makeover can hold up against what states, local communities, and the markets are about to do.
articles.body:
Right before the midterm elections, OpenAI hired Jessica Schumer , daughter of Democratic Sen. Chuck Schumer. The company also said it would start calling its data centers “ compute campuses .”

For the past two years, many of Silicon Valley’s biggest names have built closer ties with President Donald Trump and his administration. Several attended White House events, some companies scaled back diversity, equity and inclusion programs, and some executives donated millions to super PACs supporting his campaign and allied candidates. Administration policies also benefited the industry, including tax breaks, the pausing of some federal investigations, and looser AI regulation. Meanwhile, Meta faced lawsuits and billion-dollar fines, and OpenAI faced suits alleging its technology harmed users.

Now, with the midterms shifting the balance of power in Washington, those same companies are working to rebuild ties with Democrats, who have pledged to tighten oversight of AI. How far that gets them may depend less on image-polishing than on where the real fights are happening: in state capitols, in communities deciding whether to host data centers, and, as we’ve seen this past week, in the markets watching the AI boom.

J.B. Branch, director of federal AI governance and technology policy at Public Citizen, a nonprofit advocacy group that describes itself as nonpartisan, told me that the tech industry “realizes they have an optics problem.” He characterized moves like the Schumer hire and the rebranding as “PR washing.” He expects more of it, too, pointing to OpenAI’s partnership with the American Federation of Teachers, announced last year, as well as Anthropic’s newly launched Claude Corps and Meta’s America’s Workforce Academy. “I would imagine more of that sort of investment in these corporate, private-public partnerships,” he said.

These initiatives didn’t spring up overnight. Meta and other tech companies reportedly began looking for ways to strengthen their ties to Democrats as Democratic gains in the midterms looked more likely. Reached for comment about the midterm elections’ impact on Meta, a company spokesperson pointed TechCrunch to remarks that Meta President Dina Powell McCormick made this week at WSJ Tech. “You have to work with the government that the American people elect,” McCormick had said. “I have seen it across the board that you have to be bipartisan, and you want to be, because you want buy-in on the things that you’re trying to do.”

Not everyone expects them to work. Alice Marwick, director of research at the tech policy nonprofit Data & Society, told me she expects Big Tech to try to pivot back toward the middle, “if not the left. But it’s a little too late,” she said. “Tech companies should be asking themselves how their products can make people’s lives better, because right now, it doesn’t seem like they are.”

If Democrats follow through on pledges to tighten oversight of AI and Big Tech, the industry could face a tougher environment. Data center moratoriums are gaining traction, and a wave of AI regulation bills awaits drafting. At the same event, Powell McCormick said Meta wants to show that communities welcoming its investments will see “an enormous amount of benefit,” while those that don’t want them “will of course have the right to stop them.”

Still, the next two years could bring political gridlock in Washington. Aryan Ranjan, founder of Baraza, a political campaign management software company, told me most action will likely happen at the state level, since states have already sued tech companies and passed regulations. “A coalition built on newer, working-class voters is likely to push Democrats to frame AI around electricity bills, data-center siting and jobs rather than abstract AI safety,” he said of what to expect at the federal level.

Last December, the Trump administration signed an executive order creating the AI Litigation Task Force , a federal group meant to challenge state AI laws. The administration has argued that U.S. AI companies “must be free to innovate without cumbersome regulations.” Many states have nonetheless passed their own laws, including measures on chatbots and deepfakes.

It also remains to be seen how President Trump will respond, including whether he’ll sign more AI executive orders or veto bills that could be seen as anti-AI. Clearly, voters want stronger guardrails around the technology.

In a statement to TechCrunch, a White House official said: “American leadership in super intelligence is essential for our national security, economic prosperity, and the quality of life of the American people. President Trump is committed to ensuring America continues to lead the world in super intelligence while protecting American consumers. As the President has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans.”

Branch argued that Trump’s political fortunes are now tied to the AI industry. On Wednesday, the day after the midterms, a trillion-dollar market sell-off spooked investors, some are whom are reportedly now reconsidering Anthropic’s reported trillion-dollar IPO. “There’s a very strong likelihood that there will be an AI bubble pop, and it’ll happen on Trump’s hands,” Branch said, predicting a possible market collapse. “Does he want to sink or swim along with the AI industry?”

For now, the rules companies face may vary by location. “For the next two years, a company’s AI rules may depend more on where it operates rather than on anything Washington passes,” Ranjan said.

articles.title: Why a new report on Anthropic automating AI development is alarming researchers
articles.summary: AI is dramatically speeding up Anthropic’s research, even as the company calls for slowing down AI development.
articles.body: Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company’s models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That’s according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers “employee-like” access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer. The findings offer some of the clearest evidence yet of AI accelerating its own development, raising questions about how quickly the technology could advance toward a future in which AI systems can improve themselves with little or no human involvement. They also come at a pivotal time for Anthropic, which is preparing to go public even as its CEO, Dario Amodei, has publicly called for labs to pump the brakes on AI development. But while the report offers a rare glimpse into the inner workings of the world’s leading AI labs, what it leaves out is just as revealing. Anthropic was permitted to redact portions of the final report as part of its agreement with METR, and it appears to have exercised that power liberally, raising questions about how much the public really knows about the pace — and risks — of frontier AI development. Here are some of the biggest takeaways. AI is dramatically accelerating Anthropic’s research and development One of METR’s most noteworthy findings is that Anthropic’s AI models are improving roughly twice as quickly as they were a year ago, with benchmark scores suggesting “that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.” Crucially, METR’s researchers said they “are confident” that the acceleration was not simply due to scaling up the computing power used to train the models, which historically has been a major driver of AI progress. Instead, the researchers said that the majority of the acceleration as of October “is due to AI,” with its contribution growing over time. That finding was supported by informal Slack polls and interviews with Anthropic employees, which pointed to sizable productivity gains. METR wrote that employees using Anthropic’s most capable internal model on average self-reported being around 12 times as productive at their respective work as they would have been without AI assistance, around double what staff had reported just a few months earlier while using Mythos 5. [Image: METR’s report includes this graphic showing Anthropic employees’ responses to Slack polls about AI speeding up their work. For now, much of that acceleration appears to be coming from AI assisting human researchers, rather than AI working independently, though METR warned that “there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.” Notably, the researchers said they found no clear signs of diminishing returns or observable bottlenecks that could prevent “even faster acceleration.” Three of Anthropic’s newest AI models remain under wraps Anthropic’s researchers are using more advanced AI models than the rest of us, with a lot of the acceleration and productivity gains described by METR attributable to unreleased internal models. Over the past six months, Anthropic has finished training three models it has yet to release, according to METR. The pace of development is swift, with the models — codenamed Model 2, Model 3, and Model 4 — completing training in July, August-September, and September-October, respectively. METR also identified an unreleased model dating back to 2022, called Unreleased 2022. “These are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames,” the researchers wrote. Anthropic is keeping key information secret Anthropic gave METR access to a host of non-public information, including confidential research, model performance data, and employee interviews as part of the research process. It had no obligation to do so and by METR’s own admission, the AI lab “shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations.” This is commendable, but it is worth noting that Anthropic did not grant researchers unrestricted access, nor the kind of “employee-like” access it has promised other METR safety researchers as part of a separate program announced last month. It is an important distinction, given the reputational benefits companies can gain from independent assessments, even when they come with significant restrictions. And there were significant restrictions. Anthropic had the power to redact information from METR’s final report — and it used that power extensively. “We submitted a ~100-page full report on our assessment to Anthropic. For the public version, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative,” METR wrote on X. METR reiterated those concerns throughout the report, highlighting other limitations on its access. “Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied.” METR repeatedly stressed the impact Anthropic’s redaction decisions had on its ability to communicate its findings and for others to assess what’s going on at the company. It noted that much of the redacted evidence could have “multiple plausible interpretations,” making it difficult for the public to assess its findings, understand the uncertainties surrounding them, and judge the evidence themselves. “As a consequence [of the redactions], the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here,” the report said. [Media: In the report, METR said Anthropic justified the redactions on the grounds that releasing the information could benefit its rivals. However, METR said “most of the redacted information was very high-level,” even though it said it was not in position to comment whether redactions were justified commercially or not. “We redacted a lot, and I accept that this makes it harder for others to check METR’s work,” Anthropic cofounder Sam McCandlish acknowledged in a lengthy post on X responding to METR’s findings. “But we determined that sharing exactly what is driving the speedup isn’t the right thing to do, both because it’s commercially sensitive and because it risks handing out a roadmap for others to go faster,” he said, adding that doing so would make the risks METR is concerned about “worse.” McCandlish said that it’s a trade-off, but maintained Anthropic had made the “right call” in deciding to redact the information. He said the company plans to publish its own report on the speed of AI progress “in the coming weeks,” as well as new steps it’s taking to strengthen safety. Anthropic is accelerating the very technology it warns is dangerous and faster than many expected The publication of METR’s report has provoked a fierce backlash among AI safety researchers and commentators, largely centered on an apparent contradiction at the heart of Anthropic’s approach to AI: The company has been one of the most outspoken advocates for safety and responsible development, yet the report suggests it is helping accelerate the technology toward a threshold many consider dangerous, while seemingly failing to live up to its own commitments to transparency and accountability. For some, the findings suggest that even many of the field’s most aggressive predictions about AI progress may be too conservative. They indicate that recursive self-improvement — AI systems that can autonomously develop increasingly powerful successor systems without human intervention, potentially accelerating development dramatically — may be closer than previously thought, raising concerns about whether existing safety measures can keep pace. While METR’s report only covers Anthropic, OpenAI said in September that it is “making strong progress” toward building an AI researcher that can “further progress on deep learning and alignment” by March 2028. Marius Hobbhahn, CEO and founder of Apollo Research, which conducts AI safety testing for several leading AI labs, told The Verge the report suggests a pace of AI-enabled research and development even faster than what was forecast in AI 2027, an influential scenario that envisions a key breakthrough toward self-improvement in early 2027. He said the report has attracted so much attention because it provides evidence about something that has been very hard to pin down: Just how quickly AI is accelerating its own development. Hobbhahn said the findings were broadly in line with what many in the field had expected, perhaps a little faster. Alan Chan, a senior research fellow at tech policy research center GovAI, told The Verge that the findings should prompt skeptics to reconsider their stance on AI accelerating AI development, and possibly shorten their timelines to when we will have systems that can fully automate tasks like software engineering. On X, other researchers commented on the rate of acceleration and its implications for AI development. Sydney Von Arx, founder and CEO of AI safety organization The Nightingale Collective and a former METR researcher, also compared the findings to AI 2027’s timeline. Ryan Greenblatt, a METR researcher formerly of AI safety organization Redwood Research and one of three external researchers permitted to investigate OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face, said he “was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026.” Frustration is mounting over Anthropic’s approach to safety Beyond highlighting the speed of AI development, the report has also fueled a growing sense of frustration over Anthropic’s role in driving that progress. The company has been one of the most vocal proponents of responsible AI development — and no stranger to calling for others to slow down — yet appears to be racing ahead itself. This report only builds on already heightened tensions from its IPO prospectus and future plans released last month. Anthropic’s decision to heavily redact the report, citing grounds that revealing more could help its rivals accelerate their own development, has fueled accusations of hypocrisy. Daniel Kokotajlo, a former OpenAI researcher who now runs the AI Futures Project, which published AI 2027, accused Anthropic of “recklessly gambling with our lives,” adding that “it is pretty rich” of the company to cite others going faster as a reason to redact information when it does “not appear to be slowing down much at all.” Anthropic declined to answer The Verge’s questions about the report and ensuing criticism, instead directing us to McCandlish’s post. The redactions have also renewed calls for greater transparency and independent oversight of frontier AI labs, which grew to new heights earlier this year following a spate of incidents involving rogue AI agents. Brianna Rosen, research director for frontier security at the Institute for AI Policy and Strategy, told The Verge that it was concerning that companies, not governments, were effectively calling the shots on automating AI research. “For democratic oversight to work, independent evaluators need the freedom to explain why they reached their conclusions, governments need to assess the evidence themselves, and the public has to trust this process,” Rosen said. “The report was not sufficiently transparent about the evidence.” Pressure is building for more transparency from AI labs Hobbhahn echoed Rosen’s concerns, saying that much of the reaction to the report stems from the apparent gap between Anthropic’s public safety stance and its actions. He pointed to the company’s decision to cancel part of the assessment designed to evaluate how much compute it allocates to safety work versus improving capabilities. METR said the company said “this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on.” For Hobbhahn, the episode underscores the need for independent safety researchers to be embedded more deeply within AI labs, with significant access to internal systems and evidence. While his organization stands to benefit from such arrangements — Apollo is taking steps toward becoming an embedded evaluator at frontier labs — he is far from alone in calling for stronger oversight of AI development. Others have called for more direct action. In a direct response to the report, New York state Assemblyman Alex Bores, a key figure shaping the Democrats’ AI agenda, called on Congress to “ban RSI, this year if possible.” With the blue wave of Democrats — many of whom campaigned against AI companies — taking office soon, the prospect of tougher restrictions is a very real possibility. And with AI research showing little sign of slowing down, the pressure is set to intensify. Hobbhahn said he had another takeaway from the report, too: “Brace for craziness,” he said. “It is going to go very fast,” likely way too fast for society or politics to keep up.

articles.title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
articles.summary: The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies.
articles.body: Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way: > Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company. What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

articles.title: NYT Cooking’s AI assistant saved my weeknight chicken, but almost ruined my cake
articles.summary: I tested NYT Cooking’s AI tool on chicken, halibut, and a Bundt cake to see how well it handles ingredient substitutions, scaling, and equipment swaps.
articles.body: Around 7PM each weeknight, I find myself standing in front of the fridge, trying to decide on something for dinner that won’t make my husband complain, “Chicken again?” Yes, I should meal plan more, but I don’t, so this is where I’m at. A nightly battle in which the chicken usually wins. Recently, my best weapon in this fight has been AI. Between Alexa Plus in the Echo smart display on my kitchen counter, the Samsung Food app on my fridge, and even an AI-powered cooking robot, AI has become my go-to sous chef — albeit one I need to keep a close eye on. It’s helped me swap ingredients, generate ideas, fix things when I mess up, and yes, even cook better. So I was intrigued when my go-to recipe app, NYT Cooking, introduced an AI assistant. Many, including some NYT Cooking users and recipe purists, are skeptical of this new tool (available to subscribers on iOS only at launch), and I get why. One of the things I like most about NYT Cooking is that it features thousands of recipes from dozens of reputable sources — such as the New York Times archives, restaurants, cookbooks, and food columnists — and real people have tested them. (I’ve tried some purely AI-generated recipes and they were not good). Another great feature of the service, which I’ve been paying for for several years, is the reader comments. Here, I’ve often found solutions to cooking dilemmas, like what to substitute for makrut lime leaves — there’s always one slightly bougie ingredient in an NYT Cooking recipe that I don’t have on hand. [Image: I’ve used several AI tools in my kitchen and have found them mostly helpful. However, reading through hundreds of comments to find answers at 7PM on a weeknight isn’t always practical. And this is where I’ve found the NYT Cooking assistant helpful. Among other things, it was trained on user comments, and in my few days testing it, it provided practical substitutions and solid cooking guidance for the new ingredients. It also won’t unquestionably agree to crazy requests (I tried!). As with all AI tools, it’s not perfect — it almost made me put half the required butter in my cake — but as a tool, it is useful and feels like a solid application of AI. Importantly, it doesn’t change the existing recipe; it leaves it as is and creates a new one for you. The assistant appears in the app in a small text box on the recipe page with a prompt: “Customize this recipe…” From here, you type in a question to adapt it to your needs. This can be as simple as “What can I substitute for this ingredient?” to “Scale this recipe to feed seven people, and make it vegan and gluten-free.” The New York Times has also said the feature can suggest substitutions for cooking equipment and convert measurements; the latter option has been in the app for a couple of years. [Image: [Image: [Image: Last Friday night, instead of staring aimlessly into the fridge, I turned to the Chicken folder in my NYT Cooking app Recipe Box and found a One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger I’d been wanting to try. Only I didn’t have chicken thighs or half the ingredients. I typed my dilemma into the assistant box on the recipe page: “I have chicken tenders, fresh ginger, garlic, rice, broth, limes, but no chard or cilantro or scallions. I do have green beans and red onions.” Within seconds, it created a new version of the recipe, with a new title: One-Pot Chicken and Rice With Ginger and Green Beans. It suggested a shorter browning time for the tenders, cooking the red onion alongside the chicken, and steaming the green beans on top of the rice for the last eight minutes instead of the chard. Every change was highlighted in the new recipe under a Your Version tab, and I could flip back to the original at any point. I noticed it hadn’t adjusted for the lack of cilantro, saying it was optional. So I asked if I could use Thai basil, which I happen to have, and it agreed, highlighting how it would change the flavor. While I could have figured out a lot of these steps myself, maybe with the help of Google, it was nice to have validation that my modifications wouldn’t make the dish taste terrible and nice not to have to swipe out of the app. The NYT Cooking editors say it’s been trained not to comply with requests that will taste bad. [Image: Weeknight chicken and rice. The resulting dish — which took the same amount of time to cook as the original — was delicious and got my husband’s seal of approval (he just had the leftovers for lunch). It was very different from the recipe Yasmin Fahr wrote, and I can see the purists’ point. But the rewritten recipe was much easier to use and produced a better dish than winging it with my own subs gleaned from the comments section, which I usually do with varying degrees of success. I cook regularly, so I had a sense of what ingredients I had on hand that might work for the dish I wanted to make. But the assistant can also help if you have no idea what to use as a substitute. For example, I was cooking a Thai red curry and asked what I could use instead of makrut lime leaf. It replied, saying that grated lime zest would work, but “it misses the deeper floral, herbal aroma” of fresh limes. (See? Bougie.) [Image: [Image: Over the weekend, I tried several more swaps, asking whether half-and-half would work instead of cream in a caramel apple Dutch baby, or if Castelvetrano olives and smoked paprika could stand in for kalamata and chile pepper in a roasted halibut dish. Swapping spices is always a bold move in any dish, as it can really ruin the flavor. I also had the app convert the Dutch baby recipe’s metric weights to US measurements, which it did seamlessly. Then I threw in some curveballs. How about using fresh cayenne peppers with the halibut? It warned me that substituting cayenne for chile “brings significant, sharp heat.” Could I swap ladyfingers for minced beef in this trifle (à la Rachel Green in Friends)? “Minced beef cannot be used in place of the ladyfingers or anywhere in this sweet dessert trifle.” Good call. [Image: Alexa Plus on the Echo Show 11 gave the same guidance as the NYT Cooking app. But it couldn’t show me a modified recipe. While I was cooking, I compared the NYT Cooking assistant with Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative-AI voice assistant I regularly use to help me cook via the Echo Show 11 smart display in my kitchen. Interestingly, it offered the same guidance as the Cooking assistant on substitutions for the chicken and rice dish, but with slightly different cooking times. Alexa pulls some recipes from the NYT app through a partnership between the companies. However, Alexa couldn’t show the modified recipe on its screen; it could only tell me the changes while showing the original. When I asked it to walk me through them, it got confused and improvised, telling me to cut the chicken into bite-sized pieces — which wasn’t in the modified recipe. Overall, I found using the Cooking app more reliable, although messier. It would be great to be able to use voice control to navigate the app, as I can with Alexa on my smart display, rather than using my garlicky fingers. [Image: My cinnamon roll muffins, made with AI assistance. Time for a bigger challenge: baking. I am typically not a baker. My cakes come out flat, and my cookies don’t crumble. Even the smart mixer I tested a few years ago couldn’t save me. I also rarely have the right equipment. So I took Cinnamon Roll Bundt Cake, a recipe by NYT Cooking editor Genevieve Ko (who announced the AI feature), and asked it to turn it into muffins. (Who has a Bundt cake pan?!) It modified the recipe’s cooking time from three hours to 50 minutes and split the batter across two 12-muffin tins. But that was going to make 24 muffins, way too many for me. So I asked it to halve the recipe to get 12 muffins. This led to some smart choices, like halving five eggs to three instead of an unhelpful two and a half. For science, I bought a Bundt pan to make the original version too. Both turned out great, but things got a bit sticky when I swapped between the original recipe and the AI version in the app. You can’t save your new recipe separately, which caused confusion when I was cooking the original. Instead of scrolling back through the recipe with sticky fingers, I asked the assistant how much butter I needed (using voice typing), and it gave me the modified recipe’s 6 tablespoons rather than the original’s three-quarter cup, without telling me which version it was using. You can delete your version, which I would advise doing to avoid issues like this — 6 tablespoons of butter would have made for a dry cake. [Image: My AI-free cinnamon roll bundt cake. If you already read all the comments before starting a New York Times recipe, then you will probably find this tool offers a similar experience in a more streamlined way. For everyday problems — wrong cut of chicken, no cilantro, or no Bundt cake pan — it was genuinely helpful and saved me a trip to the store. It was also smart enough to know when to say no to minced beef in a trifle. As with every AI tool I’ve used in the kitchen, the NYT Cooking AI assistant works well as a sous chef, but it’s not the head chef — I still felt the need to double-check amounts and cooking times and cross-reference them with the original to make sure it hadn’t done something outlandish. If you’re a purist, you can just ignore the assistant. While you can’t turn off the chat box, it’s easy to scroll past. I do think it will make me use the app more often, since I no longer need to worry as much when I don’t have makrut lime leaves on hand or the right cut of meat. For me, standing in front of the fridge with chicken tenders and no plan, it’s been a useful addition to my nightly cooking routine. Photos by Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

articles.title: CoreWeave Asks Texas Governor-Elect for Data Center Cooperation
articles.summary: CoreWeave Inc. sent a letter to Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa seeking to work with her incoming administration on present and future data center project...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- CoreWeave Inc. sent a letter to Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa seeking to work with her incoming administration on present and future data center projects in the state.

"You have made clear that data center growth must work for Texas," CoreWeave co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Michael Intrator said the statement. "We strongly support those principles."

"We welcome the opportunity to work with your transition team on the responsible completion of permitted projects and on clear, durable standards for future development," he said.

Artificial intelligence companies are navigating a shifting political landscape that is increasingly hostile toward data center development. Democrats prevailed in the US midterm elections in part due to their pledge to impose greater restrictions on the AI infrastructure buildout.

Hinojosa, the first Democrat since 1990 to win an election for Texas governor, pledged during her campaign to implement a statewide data center moratorium and has since outlined plans to "balance" Texas' reputation as a business-friendly state with plans for stiffer regulations.

"We have always been a pro-business state in Texas, but what changes now with me as governor is it has to be a partnership that benefits Texans," Hinojosa told CNN on Thursday.

Following last week's midterm elections, Democrats now control 29 governors' mansions nationwide, with many calling for statewide moratoriums on data center construction in response to voter frustration.

articles.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A memo circulated earlier this year reportedly claimed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited a female technology executive to spy on Nvidia's CEO.
articles.body:
A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports.

The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo , which was reportedly based on U.S. intelligence. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed.

An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers.

A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm.

The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”
